documents.title: Ludork Documentation
documents.content:
# Ludork Documentation

Read this guide in the [online documentation](https://jasonleon01.github.io/Ludork/docs/v1.0/?lang=en_GB), or visit the [Ludork website](https://jasonleon01.github.io/Ludork/?lang=en_GB) for downloads and project information. The [third-party notices](https://jasonleon01.github.io/Ludork/notices/?version=1.0&lang=en_GB) are available on a separate page linked from the website footer. The documentation language and version selectors are on the right of the chapter tabs. This edition covers Ludork 1.0.

Ludork combines a visual editor, Blueprint graphs, Lua scripts and an extensible C++20 runtime for map-driven 2D games. Use the editor to configure projects and create maps, Actors, data, animation and user interfaces, then run and package the game.

![The Ludork editor workspace with a Game project map open](../../images/overview/editor-workspace.png)

*The main workspace combines the map canvas, editing modes, project data and runtime tools.*

## Choose a learning path

| If you want to… | Start here |
|---|---|
| Make a playable project | [Create Your First Project](<Getting Started/Create Your First Project.md>) |
| Author maps, assets and project data | [Start Page, Workspace and Shortcuts](<Editor User Guide/Start Page Workspace and Shortcuts.md>) |
| Configure Actor labels, lights, particles and child Actors | [Actor Components](<Editor User Guide/Actor Components/Overview.md>) |
| Look up what each Palette control does | [UI Controls in the Palette](<Editor User Guide/UI Controls in the Palette.md>) |
| Build GPU particle effects for Actors and UI | [Common Particles](<Editor User Guide/Common Particles.md>) |
| Add timed subtitles to videos | [Video Subtitles](<Editor User Guide/Video Subtitles.md>) |
| Learn Lua | [Lua Basics](<Getting Started/Lua Basics.md>) |
| Write gameplay in Lua or Blueprint | [Lua Runtime and Modules](<Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md>) |
| Add or change native runtime APIs | [Build and Module Layout](<Native C++ Development/Build and Module Layout.md>) |
| Deploy optional remote account storage | [Simple Server](<Simple Server/Deployment and Editor Settings.md>) |
| Install or write a trusted editor extension | [Installing and Managing Plug-ins](<Plug-in Development and Installation/Installing and Managing Plug-ins.md>) |
| Find unreferenced project resources | [Official Resource Cleanup](<Plug-in Development and Installation/Official Plug-ins/Resource Cleanup.md>) |

## Supported platforms

### Editors

| Platform | Minimum supported version |
|---|---|
| Windows | Windows 10, x64 |
| macOS | Apple Silicon, macOS 13.3 |

### Games

| Platform | Minimum supported version | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | Windows 10, x64 | |
| macOS | Apple Silicon, macOS 13.3 | |
| iOS | iOS 16.3, arm64 | C++ Source project required. |
| HarmonyOS | HarmonyOS 6.0.2 / API 22, arm64-v8a | Mobile and 2in1; C++ Source project required. |
| Android | Android 7.0 / API 24, arm64-v8a | C++ Source project required. |

Mobile packages are produced on Apple Silicon macOS. A Standalone project uses the prebuilt runtime for the editor’s host platform. See [Run, Debug and Package](<Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md>) for platform tools and signing options.

## Documentation conventions

- Paths are relative to the project root unless a page states otherwise.
- Menu commands and field labels are written as they appear in the English editor.
- `Code`, file names and API identifiers are case-sensitive where the underlying platform is case-sensitive.

## Product and content licences

Ludork's software licence, third-party notices and Game project asset terms are separate. Review all three before redistributing an editor package or a game made from Game project content. Installing a plug-in also runs trusted code with the permissions of the editor process. Inspect the source and origin of a plug-in before import.

documents.title: Create Your First Project
documents.content:
# Create Your First Project

Create a Standalone project, open its initial map and run it.

### Create the project

1. On the Start page, choose **New Project**.

![Ludork Start page with recent-project and project-creation actions](../../../images/getting-started/start-page.png)

*The Start page is the entry point for creating or reopening a project.*

2. Select **Standalone**.
3. Leave the FFmpeg option disabled unless the game must play video.
4. Choose an existing destination directory and enter a new project name.
5. Confirm the destination path and choose **Create**. Ludork opens `Main.proj` when creation finishes.

The first download needs an internet connection and an available template for your editor version. **Cancel** stops creation and removes unfinished files. See [Obtaining templates](<Project Templates.md#obtaining-templates>) for download and offline use.

![New Project window with the Standalone template selected](../../../images/getting-started/new-project.png)

*Standalone is the recommended first-project template because it includes a ready-to-run native runtime.*

### Save and run

1. Select a map in the map list.
2. Click **Export** to save, validate and generate the UI and locale files. Resolve any errors before continuing; Play is disabled until the first successful export.
3. Click **Play** on the toolbar. The game runs in the embedded panel or an **Individual Window**, according to **Edit → Development Tools and Settings → Individual Window**. The setting is available on Windows only. On other hosts, the game always opens in an **Individual Window**.
4. Open **Console** to see runtime output. Project editing is disabled while the game runs unless [Live Debug](<../Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md#live-debug>) was enabled before Play.
5. Click the same button, now **Stop**, to stop the game and resume editing.

A new project has no `Main.ini`; the runtime creates it on the first run. See [Project Settings and Asset Layout](<../Editor User Guide/Project Settings and Asset Layout.md>) for the project’s files and folders.

## Related pages

- [Project Templates](<Project Templates.md>)
- [Lua Basics](<Lua Basics.md>)
- [Start Page, Workspace and Shortcuts](<../Editor User Guide/Start Page Workspace and Shortcuts.md>)
- [Run, Debug and Package](<../Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md>)

documents.title: Project Templates
documents.content:
# Project Templates

## Template reference

The picker presents two template cards, **Standalone** and **C++ Source**, and an independent **Enable video playback (FFmpeg)** switch.

| Template | Native source | Native compiler required | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standalone | No | No | Authoring Lua, Blueprint, data and assets with the supplied runtime. |
| C++ Source | Yes | Yes | Changing native services, bindings or building an iOS, HarmonyOS or Android target. |

Each combination of card and switch has its own template. The template establishes the project baseline. Changing it later is a source-management task, not an editor toggle.

Before the first Play, use **Construct** for C++ Source, then **Export**. Standalone needs only Export. See [Run, Debug and Package](<../Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md>) for later builds and exports. C++ Source templates include a project-root `.clang-format` for native source formatting.

## Obtaining templates

Development editor packages include local templates. If one is missing, New Project reports an error without downloading a replacement.

Release editors obtain templates from the matching GitHub Release. Windows x64 uses ZIP archives; macOS ARM64 uses tar.gz archives. Each release provides eight separate template assets:

| Template | Windows x64 | macOS ARM64 |
|---|---|---|
| C++ Source | `game-source.zip` | `game-source.tar.gz` |
| C++ Source with FFmpeg | `game-source-ffmpeg.zip` | `game-source-ffmpeg.tar.gz` |
| Standalone | `game-standalone.zip` | `game-standalone.tar.gz` |
| Standalone with FFmpeg | `game-standalone-ffmpeg.zip` | `game-standalone-ffmpeg.tar.gz` |

Templates match the editor’s complete version, including its patch number. If a matching release or template has not been published, New Project reports that it is unavailable.

Downloaded templates are cached in `<Ludork installation directory>/Templates/v<base-version>/` on Windows and `~/Ludork/Templates/v<base-version>/` on macOS, and can be reused offline. Each project is extracted into its own directory.

New Project shows download or copy progress and extraction progress. **Cancel**, or closing the window during creation, cancels the operation and removes its unfinished project and download files. Completed, valid cache entries remain available for later use.

New Project always creates the editor's current major.minor project version, such as `v1.0` for editor `1.0.7`. It offers no older-version creation option. Opening supported older projects is a separate [project-version check](<../Editor User Guide/Project Settings and Asset Layout.md#mainproj>).

## FFmpeg option

**Enable video playback (FFmpeg)** adds local MOV and MP4 playback for H.264 video and AAC audio, and increases the build size. Other codecs, network playback and hardware acceleration are not included.

Platform preparation differs as well. Windows and macOS use shared FFmpeg libraries, while iOS, HarmonyOS and Android use static libraries. Distribution requirements, including the LGPL relinking materials for static builds, are described in `Licenses/FFmpeg/README.md`. On macOS, selecting FFmpeg also displays a compatibility notice.

## Template targets

- [Ludork Server](<../Simple Server/Deployment and Editor Settings.md>) requires C++ Source. Its Game test-server menu and Pack configuration are hidden for Standalone. All generated templates start with the server disabled and contain no test or production credentials.
- Exporting mobile packages (iOS, Android and HarmonyOS) requires a C++ Source template.
- Script compilation, shader encryption, data encryption, save encryption and **Archive Assets, Data and Scripts (.ldpak)** are packaging options, not template types. See [Run, Debug and Package](<../Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md>) for the complete option behaviour.

All four templates exclude Export outputs: `Scripts/Internal/UI/`, `Scripts/stub/Internal/UI/`, `Scripts/stub/Internal/UIWindows/`, generated locale language Lua files and `EditorCache/ProjectExport.json`. The project `.gitignore` excludes the same generated files. Templates retain UI JSON, handwritten Controllers and declarations, `Scripts/Source/Locale/Core.lua`, General Data and variable Lua with their declarations, and native binding declarations. Export creates the UI and locale files for the new project.

The retained `Scripts/stub/**/*.d.lua` files support Lua language tools. They are removed from [game packages](<../Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md#loose-and-packed-output>).

Runtime licence texts are in `Licenses`; FFmpeg variants also include `Licenses/FFmpeg`. Asset notices remain beside their assets. Packaging includes available licence texts, but their completeness remains the distributor’s responsibility.

## Related pages

- [Create Your First Project](<Create Your First Project.md>)
- [Ludork Lua Advanced](<Ludork Lua Advanced.md>)
- [Build and Module Layout](<../Native C++ Development/Build and Module Layout.md>)
- [Run, Debug and Package](<../Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md>)

documents.title: Lua Basics
documents.content:
# Lua Basics

Ludork runs Lua 5.5. This page introduces the language to readers who are new to Lua. Ludork's native additions are described separately in [Ludork Lua Advanced](<Ludork Lua Advanced.md>), and the SFML types that project Lua receives are in [SFML Quickstart](<SFML Quickstart.md>).

## Files, comments and local variables

Lua files use the `.lua` extension. `--` starts a line comment, and `--[[ ... ]]` encloses a block comment. Declare working values with `local`. An uninitialised variable is `nil`.

```lua
-- One line
local playerName = "Hero"
local level = 1
local alive = true
local target = nil
```

Lua values include `nil`, booleans, numbers, strings, functions, tables, userdata and threads. `type(value)` returns one of these built-in categories. Application objects that are represented by tables or userdata still report that underlying category.

## Operators

The common operators are:

| Kind | Operators |
|---|---|
| Arithmetic | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `//`, `%`, `^` |
| Comparison | `==`, `~=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` |
| Logic | `and`, `or`, `not` |
| Strings | `..` for concatenation |
| Length | `#value` |

Lua treats only `nil` and `false` as false. Values such as `0`, an empty string and an empty table are true in a condition.

## Conditions

```lua
if health <= 0 then
    state = "defeated"
elseif health < maxHealth then
    state = "hurt"
else
    state = "healthy"
end
```

Use explicit `nil` comparisons when absence must differ from `false`, `0` or an empty value.

## Tables

A table can act as an array, dictionary or record. Array indices start at 1.

```lua
local items = { "Key", "Potion" }
local player = {
    name = "Hero",
    hp = 100,
}

items[#items + 1] = "Gem"
player.hp = player.hp - 10
```

Assigning `nil` removes an ordinary table key. Avoid `nil` holes in arrays, because `#`, `ipairs` and array helpers stop at the first missing slot.

## Loops

```lua
for index, item in ipairs(items) do
    useItem(index, item)
end

for key, value in pairs(player) do
    inspectValue(key, value)
end

local count = 3
while count > 0 do
    count = count - 1
end
```

Use `ipairs` for dense arrays and `pairs` for dictionaries. Numeric `for` loops include both endpoints unless the step skips the last value.

## Functions and methods

Functions are values, and they may return multiple results. Define instance methods with colon syntax, which passes the receiver as `self`.

```lua
local function clampHealth(value, maximum)
    return math.max(0, math.min(value, maximum))
end

local Character = {}

function Character:setHealth(value)
    self.health = clampHealth(value, self.maxHealth)
end

local value, found = findItem("Key")
```

`object:method(value)` is equivalent to `object.method(object, value)`. Define and call instance methods with the colon form consistently.

## Modules

A module is a Lua file that returns its public value. Require it by its path below `Scripts`, using dots and no extension.

```lua
-- Scripts/Source/Score.lua
local Score = {}

function Score.Add(current, amount)
    return current + amount
end

return Score
```

```lua
local Score = require("Source.Score")

local total = Score.Add(10, 5)
```

Complete direct `require` calls before declaring aliases. Do not create directory-level `init.lua` aggregators.

## Errors

Use `assert(condition, message)` for required conditions and `error(message)` for an explicit failure. Required project data must fail at its source rather than silently produce partial state.

## Related pages

- [Ludork Lua Advanced](<Ludork Lua Advanced.md>) — classes, project truth values, native containers and Standard extensions.
- [Lua Runtime and Modules](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md>) — project module order, file layers and runtime contracts.
- [Default Template Overview](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/Default Template Overview.md>) — how the Game project uses these rules.

documents.title: Ludork Lua Advanced
documents.content:
# Ludork Lua Advanced

Ludork's Standard runtime extends Lua with native classes, containers and utility functions. These APIs are available before `Scripts/Entry.lua` and do not require a `Standard` module. They are distinct from the `Engine`, `GlobalCore`, `GlobalFunctions` and LuaSF bindings documented in API Reference.

Exact development-time signatures are declared in `Scripts/stub/Standard.d.lua` and `Scripts/stub/Class.d.lua`.

## Ludork classes

Create a plain definition table without a metatable, add defaults and methods, then return `class(definition, ...)`. The definition must not already be finalised. Every base must be a finalised Ludork class or a registered native type. Duplicate bases are rejected. Base order determines the C3 method-resolution order.

```lua
local Engine = require("Engine")

local Actor = Engine.Actor

local Pickup = {}

Pickup.count = 1
Pickup.sound = ""

function Pickup:init(texture, tag)
    Actor.init(self, texture, tag)
    self._collected = false
end

return class(Pickup, Actor)
```

### Defaults and instance state

Editable or inheritable defaults belong on the definition table before finalisation. This includes metadata fields, component defaults, `default*` spawn values and Blueprint-overridable identifiers.

`init` applies constructor arguments and creates per-instance state. Copy mutable class defaults when each instance must own an independent value:

```lua
local RouteFollower = {}

RouteFollower.speed = 96.0
RouteFollower.defaultRoute = {}

function RouteFollower:init()
    self._route = deepcopy(self.defaultRoute)
    self._routeIndex = 1
end

return class(RouteFollower)
```

Do not initialise a public default only inside `init`. Subclasses and Blueprint discovery read it from the class.

An explicit `nil` restored from Blueprint, Component or General Data is an own field that overrides inherited defaults. Inheritance, `copy` and `deepcopy` preserve it. Assigning `nil` in Lua clears that override and resumes inheritance lookup. Native properties and Lua getters and setters keep their existing behaviour.

### Construction, lifecycle and inheritance

`Type.new(...)` constructs an instance and calls `init`. Finalised classes are also callable, but project code follows the style of the neighbouring module. A class without `init` accepts no arguments unless a single native root defines the constructor contract. Invoke required native-base initialisers explicitly. Lifecycle methods such as `onCreate`, `onTick` and `onDestroy` run only when their owning runtime contract calls them. `instance:dispose()` runs the resolved implementation at most once, releases native ownership and instance fields, and is not repeated by garbage collection.

Before a native root is constructed, typed assignments to its properties are stored on the composite and applied during native-base initialisation. Native property access uses that root; script getters and setters are resolved from script classes. Setter errors propagate to the caller.

Inside a method, `super()` resolves the next implementation from the defining class. Use `super(ClassName, self)` when an indirect callback makes ownership ambiguous. Multiple inheritance is supported, and declared base order must remain stable.

Direct Script Mixins follow their separate lifecycle and must not declare `init`.

### Class utilities

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Class.isInstance(value, target)` | Test a raw Lua type or an instance against a class's complete MRO. |
| `Class.isSubclass(value, target)` | Test a class against its complete MRO. |
| `Class.type(value)` | Return its Ludork class or native fallback type. |
| `Class.hasOwnField(value, key)` | Test whether a field is stored directly. |
| `Class.getMro(value)` | Return a detached MRO array. |
| `Class.getParameterNames(callable)` | Return declared parameter names without `self`. |
| `Class.constructNamed(type, values)` | Match named values to `init` parameters and construct. |
| `Class.super(cls?, self?)` / `super(...)` | Resolve the next implementation in the active MRO. |
| `Class.monitor` / `Class.unmonitor` | Add or remove a named subscription to a field. |
| `Class.MISSING` | Sentinel used when a monitored field had no previous value. |

`Class.monitor(target, name, callback, params?, notifyEqualWrites?, identifier?)` subscribes to a table or userdata field without immediately invoking the callback. `identifier` defaults to `""`. The same identifier replaces its subscription in place, while different identifiers run in registration order. `Class.unmonitor(target, name, identifier?)` removes only that subscription. A missing subscription is ignored. Omitting the identifier retains the single-subscription behaviour.

Monitored fields reject `nil` assignments and normally notify only when their visible value changes. Pass `true` as `notifyEqualWrites` to receive equal writes for that subscription. A previous missing or explicit `nil` value reports `Class.MISSING`. Each callback receives `(oldValue, newValue, ...)`, followed by the entries of `params`. Re-entrant assignments take effect, but each subscription suppresses its own recursion. Callback errors stop dispatch and propagate without rolling back the assignment.

Dispatch uses a subscription snapshot. Removing or replacing a subscription before its turn skips the old callback, and newly registered callbacks start with subsequent assignments. The removal of the last subscription restores ordinary field storage and the original metatable of the table.

### Type checks

Use `Class.isInstance` for every type check. Its target may be a finalised Ludork or registered native class, or an exact Lua type name: `nil`, `boolean`, `number`, `string`, `function`, `userdata`, `thread` or `table`.

```lua
if Class.isInstance(value, "string") then
    print(string.upper(value))
end

local isActor = Class.isInstance(actor, Actor)
local isNativeVector = Class.isInstance(position, sf.Vector2f)
local isInteger = Class.isInstance(value, "number") and math.type(value) == "integer"
```

String targets preserve Lua `type` semantics: native containers are userdata, and callable tables remain tables. Unknown names return false. Targets that are neither strings nor tables are argument errors. Use `math.type` only after a number check, and `Class.type` only when the resolved type value is needed. Never compare Lua `type` with `==` or `~=`.

## Project truth values and copies

Lua itself treats only `nil` and `false` as false. Ludork's `bool(value)` additionally treats `0`, empty strings, empty tables and empty native containers as false. Use explicit `nil` comparisons only when absence is a distinct protocol value.

| API | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `copy(value)` | Shallow-copy tables and supported native values. |
| `deepcopy(value)` | Recursively copy keys and values while preserving aliases and cycles. |
| `asizeof(value)` | Estimate the memory owned by a Lua or native value graph, in bytes. |

For known bound value types, use `value:copy()` or `value:deepcopy()` directly, for example `position:copy()`, `rect:copy()` and `colour:copy()`. These methods produce independent values. Global `copy` and `deepcopy` serve Lua tables and dynamic value graphs; when they encounter a supported bound value, they use the same LuaGlue copy entry points. Resources without a value-copy policy retain identity.

For monitored tables, `copy` and `deepcopy` copy the current logical field values and preserve the original metatable, without the monitoring proxy or subscriptions. The copied values can be saved normally. Subscriptions belong to live instances and must be registered again after loading.

## Native containers

`list`, `tuple` and `dict` are native containers. They do not replace the Lua tables required by JSON, metadata, Blueprint values or Core bindings.

```lua
local route = list("north", nil, "east")
local position = tuple(4, 7)
local visited = dict {
    [position] = true,
}
```

`list(...)` and `tuple(...)` store arguments as 1-based slots. A single table, list or tuple argument is shallow-copied as a sequence. `dict(mapping?)` copies a mapping. Tuples reject `nil`. Lists and dictionaries preserve `nil` slots or values. Negative sequence indices are invalid. List writes and inserts must target an existing slot or `#value + 1`.

| Type | Main operations |
|---|---|
| `list` | `append`, `extend`, `insert`, `pop`, `remove`, `clear`, `index`, `count`, `contains`, `reverse`, `sort`, `copy`, `unpack`, `toTable` |
| `tuple` | `index`, `count`, `contains`, `unpack`, `toTable` |
| `dict` | `get`, `setdefault`, `update`, `pop`, `remove`, `clear`, `contains`, `keys`, `values`, `items`, `copy`, `toTable` |

Native `ipairs` visits `nil` list slots, and dictionary iteration preserves insertion order. Structural mutation during iteration fails. `dict:get(key, default)` uses the default only for a missing key, and `dict:contains(key)` distinguishes that case from a stored `nil` value. Remove entries with `remove` or `pop`, not `dictionary[key] = nil`. `remove` returns whether it found the key. `pop` raises for a missing key unless given a default.

`list:pop()` removes the last slot by default. `list:remove` raises when its value is absent, and `list:sort(compare?)` is stable. Dictionary `keys` and `values` return insertion-ordered list snapshots. `items` is a lazy iterator. Dictionary method names take precedence over same-named string keys in direct lookup, so read such an entry with `value:get("get")` or `dict.get(value, "get")`.

Lists and dictionaries compare structurally, including cyclic graphs. Tuples are immutable native-dictionary keys. Booleans, finite numbers, strings and nested tuples compare by value, while mutable or reference values compare by identity. `nil` and non-finite numeric tuple keys are invalid. Ordinary Lua tables still hash tuple userdata by identity.

### Conversion boundaries

`toTable` recursively converts native containers while preserving aliases and cycles. Converted lists and tuples retain JSON-array shape when empty or nested. `nil` list slots and dictionary values become `cjson.null`. Tuple keys become compact strings such as `(1,2)` and fail on collision with an existing string key. JSON encoders, metadata, Blueprint values and Core bindings do not perform this conversion automatically.

Use record arrays instead when key identity must be reconstructed after loading.

## Math extensions

Standard adds the following functions to Lua's `math` library. Except for `isFinite`, arguments must be finite Lua numbers. Convert numeric strings explicitly with `tonumber`. Invalid ranges, arithmetic overflow and integer results outside the Lua integer range raise errors. `gcd` and `lcm` require Lua integers. `round` and `trunc` preserve integer inputs exactly.

`lerp`, `inverseLerp` and `remap` support reversed intervals and extrapolation without clamping.

| API | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `math.isFinite(value)` | Return true for finite Lua numbers, false otherwise. |
| `math.clamp(value, min, max)` | Return a float constrained to `[min, max]`. Require `min <= max`. |
| `math.lerp(a, b, t)` | Linearly interpolate from `a` to `b` by `t`. |
| `math.round(value)` | Round to the nearest integer, choosing the even integer at exact halves. |
| `math.trunc(value)` | Truncate toward zero and return an integer, unlike the exact conversion in `math.tointeger`. |
| `math.isNearZero(value, epsilon=0.1)` | Test `abs(value) < epsilon`. Require `epsilon >= 0`. |
| `math.gcd(a, b)` | Return the nonnegative greatest common divisor. `gcd(0, 0)` is 0. |
| `math.lcm(a, b)` | Return the nonnegative least common multiple, or 0 if either argument is 0. |
| `math.sign(value)` | Return the integer −1, 0 or 1. Both signed zeros return 0. |
| `math.inverseLerp(a, b, value)` | Return `(value - a) / (b - a)`. Require `a ~= b`. |
| `math.remap(value, inMin, inMax, outMin, outMax)` | Map proportionally from the input interval to the output interval. Require `inMin ~= inMax`. |
| `math.smoothstep(edge0, edge1, value)` | Clamp the normalised position `t` to `[0, 1]`, then return `t²(3 − 2t)`. Require `edge0 < edge1`. |
| `math.moveTowards(current, target, maxDelta)` | Move by at most `maxDelta` without passing the target. Require `maxDelta >= 0`. |

## String and table extensions

Standard adds these helpers to Lua's existing libraries:

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `string.pformat` | Format `{}` positional fields or `{name}` fields from a final mapping table. `{{` and `}}` escape braces. |
| `string.contains`, `string.startsWith`, `string.endsWith` | Test string contents or boundaries. |
| `string.isEmpty`, `string.isBlank` | Test empty or whitespace-only text. |
| `string.strip`, `string.stripLeading`, `string.stripTrailing` | Remove Unicode whitespace. |
| `string.replace`, `string.split` | Replace or split text. |
| `string.utf8Length`, `string.utf8Slice` | Measure or slice by UTF-8 codepoints. |
| `string.graphemeLength` | Count Unicode grapheme clusters (user-perceived characters). |
| `string.stripUnicode` | Trim Unicode White_Space from both ends. |
| `table.contains`, `table.index` | Search a dense Lua array using Lua equality. Stop at its first `nil` slot. |
| `table.orderedStringKeys` | Return preferred keys first, then remaining string keys sorted. |

## Platform, configuration and files

`PLATFORM` is the lower-case target name (`win32`, `darwin`, `ios`, `android`, `ohos` or the CMake system name). `LUDORK_MOBILE` and `LUDORK_DESKTOP` expose the runtime host category. Do not infer a platform from paths or environment variables.

`configparser.ConfigParser()` reads and writes INI data. It provides `read`, `write`, `has_section`, `add_section`, `get`, `getfloat`, `getint`, `getboolean` and `set`. `locale.getdefaultlocale()` returns the host locale pair.

Filesystem extensions are:

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `os.getcwd`, `os.listdir` | Read the current directory, or sorted direct entries. |
| `os.createDirectories` | Create a UTF-8 directory path and its missing parents. Existing directories are accepted. |
| `os.removeFile` | Remove one UTF-8 file path. Missing files and failures raise. This does not replace `os.remove`. |
| `os.path.join`, `os.path.splitext`, `os.path.basename`, `os.path.dirname`, `os.path.abspath` | Build or inspect paths. |
| `os.path.isdir`, `os.path.isfile` | Test existing directory or file paths. Missing paths return false, and inspection errors propagate. |
| `os.path.getmtime` | Return a file modification timestamp. |

Join `os.listdir` names to their parent before testing them.

`os.listdir`, `os.path.isdir`, `os.path.isfile` and `io.open` use only the real filesystem. `/Game/Assets/...` works only with Ludork resource APIs. For packed Data, `os.path.getmtime("Data/...")` returns the timestamp of the containing `.ldpak` file. Other filesystem APIs do not expose archive entries.

Standard also installs binary-safe codec globals:

| API | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `zlib.compress`, `zlib.decompress` | Compress data to zlib, or decompress zlib or gzip data. |
| `base64.encode`, `base64.decode` | Encode or decode Base64. Decoding accepts whitespace and valid padding, and rejects malformed data. |

## Cooperative tasks and file batches

`asyncio.create_task(callback, ...)` starts a cooperative task. Inside it, use `asyncio.sleep(seconds)` for a delay or `asyncio.await(operation)` to wait for an asynchronous result without blocking the game loop. Both require a task created by `asyncio.create_task`.

For example, while a `SceneMap` is active, these configured tutorials run in order:

```lua
local Scene = require("GlobalFunctions.Scene")

local task = asyncio.create_task(function ()
    asyncio.await(Scene.ShowTutorial("Map01Menu"))
    asyncio.await(Scene.ShowTutorial("Map01Dialogue"))
    asyncio.await(Scene.ShowMessage("Guide", "Ready to continue."))
end)
```

`await` returns the operation's final result. If the operation is cancelled, the task ends without running the next statement. To stop only this task, call `asyncio.cancel_task(task)`; the shared operation and its other waiters remain active. Task completion and cancellation run Lua `__close` cleanup.

See [AsyncOperation](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Events and Module Root.md#asyncoperation>) for the operation API and [Lua Runtime and Modules](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md#asynchronous-operation-updates>) for custom-entry initialisation.

For larger reads, `asyncio.start_file_batch(specs)` scans and reads at most four files concurrently while preserving manifest order. Logical `Data/...` roots support packed Data. Other roots use the physical filesystem. `asyncio.poll_file_batch(job, maxItems?)` returns progress, delivered items and a structured failure. `asyncio.cancel_file_batch(job)` cancels the job.

With `parseData = true`, the suffix must end in `.json` or `.ldc`; workers decode JSON or binary LDC and polling returns a `FileBatchDataConversion`. Decode failures use `operation = "parse"`. Advance the conversion on the Lua logic thread with `asyncio.step_file_batch_data(conversion, maxNodes, maxMilliseconds)`, using positive budgets. It returns `completed, processed, data`, with data delivered once on completion. Arrays carry their logical length in `n`; root null is nil, null array slots are absent keys, and null object fields retain `cjson.null`, matching `Engine.loadData`. `contentBytes` is the decoded payload byte count, before conversion into Lua values. `asyncio.clear_file_batch_data` releases the conversion idempotently. Cancellation, collection and shutdown also invalidate it. Conversions cannot cross Lua VMs or threads.

Without `parseData`, `item.content` contains the original file bytes, including the LDC header and encoded payload. Pass them to `Engine.decodeData` when the data is needed. Blueprint caches retain these bytes for deferred decoding.

## Timing and memory diagnostics

`perfCounter()` returns a monotonic high-resolution time in seconds. `processMemoryMB()` returns current process memory in MiB. Use `asizeof` for an owned value graph rather than process-wide memory.

## Related pages

- [Lua Basics](<Lua Basics.md>)
- [SFML Quickstart](<SFML Quickstart.md>)
- [Lua Runtime and Modules](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md>)
- [Script Mixin Runtime Contract](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Script Mixins/Runtime Contract.md>)
- [Engine: Events and Module Root](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Events and Module Root.md>)

documents.title: SFML Quickstart
documents.content:
# SFML Quickstart

SFML is the multimedia library behind the Ludork runtime. It supplies the graphics, audio, window and input layer, and Ludork projects use its value types for positions, sizes, colours and rectangles.

Ludork embeds SFML through LuaSF, which registers the global `sf` table. Every project script can use it without a `require`.

## Official documentation

| Resource | Address |
|---|---|
| SFML 3.1.0 API reference | <https://www.sfml-dev.org/documentation/3.1.0/> |
| SFML 3.1 tutorials | <https://www.sfml-dev.org/tutorials/3.1/> |
| SFML project home | <https://www.sfml-dev.org/> |
| SFML source repository | <https://github.com/SFML/SFML> |

The repository vendors **SFML 3.1.0**. Online material for SFML 2 is still common and uses a different constructor style, so prefer the 3.1 pages above.

## What Ludork provides and what SFML provides

Ludork does not hide SFML; it builds on top of it. The two layers have different jobs.

| Layer | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Ludork | Project data, maps, Actors, Blueprints, Scenes, the declarative UI asset system, resource managers and packaging. |
| SFML | Graphics, audio, windowing, input devices and the geometry and value types those subsystems exchange. |

Use `sf` for graphics values and resources, and `Engine`, `GlobalCore` or `GlobalFunctions` for maps, Actors, Blueprints and project data.

Most drawing in a project goes through Engine controls and Scenes rather than a hand-built `sf.RenderWindow`, because the runtime owns the window, the frame loop and the UI tree. The SFML layer is where the underlying values and resources come from.

## The sf table

`sf` is a plain global table of classes, enums and helper functions. The full declaration is in `Scripts/stub/LuaSF.d.lua`, which the EmmyLua workspace indexes, so completion and hover work inside the editor.

| sf group | Members |
|---|---|
| Vector and matrix | `sf.Vector2i`, `sf.Vector2u`, `sf.Vector2f`, `sf.Vector2b`, `sf.Vector3i`, `sf.Vector3u`, `sf.Vector3f`, `sf.Vector3b`, `sf.Vector4i`, `sf.Vector4f`, `sf.Vector4b`, `sf.Mat3`, `sf.Mat4`, and the GLSL aliases `sf.Vec2`, `sf.Vec3`, `sf.Vec4`, `sf.Ivec2`, `sf.Ivec3`, `sf.Ivec4`, `sf.Bvec2`, `sf.Bvec3`, `sf.Bvec4` |
| Geometry | `sf.Color`, `sf.IntRect`, `sf.FloatRect`, `sf.Angle`, `sf.Time`, `sf.Transform` |
| Graphics | `sf.Texture`, `sf.Image`, `sf.Font`, `sf.Text`, `sf.Shader`, `sf.RenderStates`, `sf.RenderTarget`, `sf.RenderTexture`, `sf.RenderWindow`, `sf.VertexArray`, `sf.VertexBuffer`, `sf.Vertex`, `sf.Shape`, `sf.CircleShape`, `sf.ConvexShape`, `sf.RectangleShape`, `sf.Sprite`, `sf.View` |
| Audio | `sf.SoundBuffer`, `sf.Sound`, `sf.Music`, `sf.SoundStream`, `sf.SoundSource`, `sf.Listener`, `sf.SoundRecorder`, `sf.SoundChannel`, `sf.PlaybackDevice` |
| Window and input | `sf.Keyboard`, `sf.Mouse`, `sf.Joystick`, `sf.Touch`, `sf.Sensor`, `sf.Clipboard`, `sf.Cursor`, `sf.VideoMode`, `sf.Event` and its `sf.Event_*` variants |
| System | `sf.Clock`, `sf.sleep`, `sf.Version`, `sf.InputStream`, `sf.FileInputStream`, `sf.MemoryInputStream` |
| Network | `sf.IpAddress`, `sf.Dns`, `sf.Http`, `sf.Ftp`, `sf.Sftp`, `sf.TcpSocket`, `sf.TcpListener`, `sf.UdpSocket`, `sf.SocketSelector`, `sf.Packet` |

Helpers sit directly on `sf`: `sf.seconds`, `sf.milliseconds` and `sf.microseconds` build an `sf.Time`, while `sf.degrees` and `sf.radians` build an `sf.Angle`. Named blend modes such as `sf.BlendAlpha` and `sf.BlendAdd` are also `sf` fields.

## Value types

Geometry values are native userdata, not Lua tables. Compare them with the Standard `list`, `tuple` and `dict` containers, which are a separate system and are not SFML values.

Construct them with `new`:

```lua
local cell = sf.Vector2i.new(4, 7)
local speed = sf.Vector2f.new(1.5, -2.5)
local limit = sf.Vector2u.new(640, 480)
local tint = sf.Color.new(255, 255, 255, 128)
local area = sf.IntRect.new(0, 0, 32, 32)
```

`x` and `y` are readable and writable fields, and `Vector3*` and `Vector4*` add `z` and `w`:

```lua
local position = sf.Vector2i.new(0, 0)
position.x = position.x + 1
position.y = 4

local amount = sf.Vector3f.new(1.0, 0.5, 0.0)
local offset = sf.Vector4f.new(0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0)
```

Two-dimensional vectors support arithmetic operators, so movement and centring read naturally:

```lua
local start = sf.Vector2f.new(64.0, 64.0)
local step = sf.Vector2f.new(16.0, 0.0)

local moved = start + step * 2.0   -- Vector2f(96, 64)
local back = moved - step
local mirrored = -moved
local half = moved / 2.0

local isSame = moved == back + step -- true
```

Operators are `+`, `-`, unary `-`, `*` and `/` by a scalar number, and `==`. Only `==` is defined, so ordering comparisons such as `<` are not available on vectors. Multiplication between two vectors is a method rather than an operator. `lengthSquared`, `perpendicular`, `dot`, `cross`, `componentWiseMul`, `componentWiseDiv` and `unpack` exist on all three `Vector2` types, and `unpack` returns the components as separate values. The floating-point type adds `length`, `normalized`, `angle`, `angleTo`, `rotatedBy` and `projectedOnto`, which works in `sf.Angle` rather than degrees.

`sf.Vector2f.new` also accepts a length and an `sf.Angle`, which builds the vector from polar coordinates:

```lua
local forward = sf.Vector2f.new(1.0, sf.degrees(90)) -- Vector2f(0, 1)
```

### Colour, rectangles and time

`sf.Color` holds `r`, `g`, `b` and `a` in the range 0 to 255. The four-argument constructor takes red, green, blue and alpha, and shorter forms default the missing components:

```lua
local solid = sf.Color.new(32, 96, 160)
local veil = sf.Color.new(0, 0, 0, 160)
```

Predefined colours are fields of `sf.Color`: `Black`, `White`, `Red`, `Green`, `Blue`, `Yellow`, `Cyan`, `Magenta` and `Transparent`. `toInteger` returns the packed 32-bit value. `sf.Color` has no operators, so it cannot be added or compared; read and compare its components if that is needed.

`sf.IntRect.new` and `sf.FloatRect.new` take a position and a size, and both also accept four numbers. The last two numbers are width and height, not the bottom-right corner:

```lua
local tile = sf.IntRect.new(sf.Vector2i.new(0, 0), sf.Vector2i.new(32, 32))
local same = sf.IntRect.new(0, 0, 32, 32)
local sub = sf.IntRect.new(32, 0, 32, 32)

local origin = tile.position      -- Vector2i(0, 0)
local height = tile.size.y        -- 32
local inside = tile.contains(sf.Vector2i.new(16, 16)) -- true
local overlap = tile.findIntersection(sub) -- an sf.IntRect, or nil, when the rectangles do not overlap
```

`sf.Angle` carries a rotation. It is not a number, so an angle value has to go through `sf.degrees` or `sf.radians` rather than being passed as degrees:

```lua
local facing = sf.degrees(90)
local radians = sf.radians(math.pi / 2)

local degrees = facing.asDegrees()
local wrapped = sf.degrees(450).wrapSigned().asDegrees() -- 90
```

`wrapSigned` constrains an angle to `[-180°, 180°)` and `wrapUnsigned` to `[0°, 360°)`. Both are optional: an angle outside those ranges is still valid, so use them only when a comparison or a normalised display value needs the constrained form. `sf.Angle.new()` and `sf.Angle.Zero` are both zero.

`sf.Time` carries a duration, and `sf.seconds`, `sf.milliseconds` and `sf.microseconds` build one:

```lua
local cooldown = sf.seconds(0.75)

local milliseconds = cooldown.asMilliseconds() -- 750
```

`sf.Time.new()` is zero as well; `sf.sleep` pauses the calling thread for a duration.

## Object types

The graphics objects follow the SFML hierarchy, and Lua sees the same relationships:

```text
sf.Drawable
sf.Transformable
sf.Shape : sf.Drawable, sf.Transformable
sf.CircleShape, sf.ConvexShape, sf.RectangleShape : sf.Shape
sf.Sprite : sf.Drawable, sf.Transformable
sf.Text : sf.Drawable, sf.Transformable
```

Every `sf.Transformable` exposes `setPosition` and `getPosition` with `sf.Vector2f`, `setRotation` and `getRotation` with `sf.Angle`, `setScale`, `getScale`, `setOrigin` and `getOrigin` with `sf.Vector2f`, plus `move`, `rotate`, `scale` and `getTransform`.

```lua
local cell = sf.RectangleShape.new(sf.Vector2f.new(32.0, 32.0))

cell:setPosition(sf.Vector2f.new(64.0, 64.0))
cell:setOrigin(sf.Vector2f.new(16.0, 16.0))
cell:setRotation(sf.degrees(45))
cell:setScale(sf.Vector2f.new(2.0, 2.0))
cell:move(sf.Vector2f.new(8.0, 0.0))

local bounds = cell:getGlobalBounds()
```

`sf.RectangleShape.new` takes a size, `sf.CircleShape.new` takes a radius and a point count, `sf.ConvexShape.new` takes a point count, and `sf.Text.new` takes a font, a string and a character size. Shapes also carry `setFillColor` and `setOutlineColor` with an `sf.Color`, and `setOutlineThickness` with a number.

The abstract bases above are present as tables but have no `new`: `sf.Drawable`, `sf.Shape`, `sf.RenderTarget`, `sf.InputStream`, `sf.SoundSource`, `sf.SoundStream`, `sf.SoundRecorder`, `sf.SoundFileReader`, `sf.SoundFileWriter` and `sf.Socket` cannot be constructed. Create a concrete subclass instead, and treat the base as the type a parameter or a return value declares. `sf.Drawable` is the one exception that Lua can implement: `sf.LuaDrawable.new(drawCallback)` produces a drawable whose `draw` runs in Lua.

Events follow the same pattern in reverse. The payload types such as `sf.Event_Closed` and `sf.Event_Resized` are constructible, while `sf.Event.new` requires one of them as its argument. Project code normally receives events instead of building them.

## Using SFML in a project

Positions, sizes and rectangles travel across the Engine API as `sf` values, so converting between cell coordinates and world positions is ordinary vector arithmetic:

```lua
local Player = require("GlobalFunctions.Player")

local CELL_SIZE = Engine.GetCellSize()

local function cellToWorld(cellX, cellY)
    return sf.Vector2f.new(cellX * CELL_SIZE, cellY * CELL_SIZE)
end

local player = Player.GetPlayer()
if player ~= nil then
    local position = player:getPosition()
    local cell = sf.Vector2i.new(
        math.floor(position.x / CELL_SIZE),
        math.floor(position.y / CELL_SIZE)
    )
end
```

Check the declared type before passing a value. An API that declares `sf.Vector2f` does not accept a `sf.Vector2i`, a Standard `tuple` or a plain table, and it does not convert one for you.

JSON and metadata hold pure data, while `sf` values are native userdata, so converting between the two forms is explicit rather than automatic. The Game project's save codec writes a `sf.Vector2i` as `{ x, y }` and rebuilds it on load, and its record normaliser turns `sf.Vector2i`, `sf.Vector3i`, `sf.IntRect`, `sf.FloatRect` and `sf.Color` into numeric arrays. Store the components whenever the destination is data, and build the `sf` value again where it is used.

## Where to read more

- `Scripts/stub/LuaSF.d.lua` is the complete declaration of everything under `sf`, with the SFML documentation comment carried across.
- The [SFML 3.1.0 API reference](<https://www.sfml-dev.org/documentation/3.1.0/>) describes the C++ side of the same classes. Names and argument order match closely, so it is the best place to look up a member this page does not list.
- The [SFML 3.1 tutorials](<https://www.sfml-dev.org/tutorials/3.1/>) explain the concepts behind sprites, textures, views, shaders and audio.

## Related pages

- [Lua Basics](<Lua Basics.md>)
- [Ludork Lua Advanced](<Ludork Lua Advanced.md>)
- [Engine: Gameplay Types](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Gameplay Types.md>)
- [Build and Module Layout](<../Native C++ Development/Build and Module Layout.md>)

documents.content:
# Start Page, Workspace and Shortcuts

## Start page

The Start page lists up to three recently opened projects and provides **New Project** and **Open Project**. Opening a validated `.proj` file moves it to the top of the list. The Start page removes unavailable entries as it loads. Opening `Main.proj` replaces the current project only after the unsaved-work checks succeed.

Dropping an existing `.proj` file anywhere on the Start page opens it. When several files are dropped, the editor uses the first existing `.proj` file and ignores the others.

An unsupported project version cannot be opened. See [Main.proj](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md#mainproj>) for supported versions.

## Main workspace

The main window contains the map list, map canvas, editing-mode inspector and **World Outliner**, with **File Explorer**, **Actor Library** and **Console** tabs below. Tile and Actor mode controls sit beside the canvas and are hidden for world maps. The toolbar provides **Construct → Export → Play** / **Stop**; Standalone projects hide Construct. See [Run, Debug and Package](<Run Debug and Package.md>).

Resource windows display a loading indicator while opening. If loading fails, use **Retry**.

![The Ludork main workspace with its map and project panels](../../../images/overview/editor-workspace.png)

*The visible inspector and canvas interaction change with the selected editing mode.*

## Online documentation

**F1** opens the online manual inside the editor. The installed editor version selects its matching major.minor documentation: 1.0.7 opens `/Ludork/docs/v1.0/`. The current editor language is selected initially; language and version selectors remain available beside the chapter tabs. About and third-party notices also load online, while About retains the installed package version.

The embedded pages hide website navigation. Documentation links stay in the window; the homepage, downloads and external links open in the system browser. An internet connection is required. Failed page loads offer **Retry**. Windows requires Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime and offers an installation link when it is missing; macOS uses its system WKWebView.

## Global editor preferences

`Ludork.ini` stores preferences shared by all projects and restores them when the editor starts.

| Area | Saved preferences |
|---|---|
| Main window | Normal position and size, maximised state, map-list and inspector widths, lower-area height, Actor outliner/inspector proportions and the world-map child-list width. |
| File Explorer | Icon/list view, content zoom, expanded/collapsed source list and preferred external open target. |
| Actor Library | Icon/list view. |
| Tool windows | Position, normal size and maximised state for each window type. |
| Tool content | Existing adjustable split widths or proportions, the UI timeline and system-control category expansion, and particle configuration section expansion. |

Defaults are icon view in both panels, 100% File Explorer zoom, a collapsed source list and the system file manager. Missing or invalid preferences use defaults. Project browsing and map selection stay in `Main.proj`; global preferences do not modify project resources or restore search text, input drafts, layer selection or canvas view state.

Window layouts adapt to the current monitors. For each window type, the most recent adjustment is restored; minimised state is not restored.

[Viewport Options](<Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md#viewport>) are saved immediately in the project's `Main.proj` under `editor.mapViewport` and restored when the project is reopened. Projects without saved options start in Unlit with Realtime, fog, panorama and Actor origins enabled, and light bounds disabled.

## Global shortcuts

The primary modifier is `Ctrl` on Windows and `Command` on macOS.

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl/Command+N` | New Project |
| `Ctrl/Command+O` | Open Project |
| `Ctrl/Command+S` | Save |
| `Ctrl/Command+Z` | Undo |
| `Ctrl/Command+Shift+Z` or `Ctrl/Command+Y` | Redo |
| `Ctrl/Command+W` | Exit or close the project window |
| `Ctrl/Command+1` | Tile mode |
| `Ctrl/Command+2` | Actor mode |
| `F1` | Ludork Documentation |
| `F3` | Game Config |
| `F4` | System Config |
| `F5` | Animation Overview |
| `F6` | Common Particle Overview |
| `F7` | Tilesets Data |
| `F8` | Common Functions |
| `F9` | Game Variables |
| `F10` | General Data |

Some document windows add context-specific shortcuts. In the Blueprint editor, `F2` renames the selected event tab. In the Common Functions window it renames the selected Common Function, in the file explorer it renames the selected file, except on macOS, and in the animation editor it renames the selected time tag. No window displays an `F2` hint.

Single-button hint and error dialogs close with `Enter`, `Return`, `Space` or `Escape`. In confirmation dialogs, `Enter`, `Return` and `Space` confirm the action, while `Escape` cancels it.

## Editing and saving

Displayed field defaults are written only when the field is edited.

File fields that can be cleared offer **Clear** as the first item in the file selector, in every directory and for every file filter. Select it and choose **Open**, press Enter or double-click it to clear the field. **Cancel** or Escape keeps the previous value. Save dialogs, multi-file imports and selectors that require an actual file do not offer this item.

Managed resource changes stay in memory until Save. All Save buttons and `Ctrl/Command+S` write every modified document, including unopened resources, and Construct, Export, Play and Pack use the same workflow. Successful saves show no result dialog; a failed save reports only the failed items and their errors. Normal Save validates changed Blueprints, while forced saving can retain unfinished graphs. [Game Config](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md#mainini>) writes immediately on confirmation.

Saving and renaming resources temporarily disable editing, project switching and window closing. Longer operations show progress and cannot be cancelled. If project data changes during an operation, the editor asks you to retry.

Undo and Redo apply only to the active file, which keeps its 100 most recent entries. Windows that show the same file share its data and history, including after they are closed and reopened. Continuous text or numeric input in one field merges into a single step. Changing the control or the editing view, an automatic update, Save, Undo and Redo all end that step. Buttons, check boxes and selections each remain separate steps.

Undo cannot restore a reference to a deleted resource; a rejected step leaves the document and history unchanged.

Automatic reference updates create a marked Undo barrier in every changed target file, including unopened files. Later edits remain undoable, but Undo cannot cross the barrier and reports the barrier's source. Undoing or redoing the source rename updates references against the current target content and adds a new barrier, which preserves unrelated edits. Saving preserves the history and the barriers, so Undo can mark a saved file as modified again.

Modified files show `*` in the file explorer and in editor titles, and they are marked in resource selectors. Closing or replacing a project lists unsaved files and offers **Save**, **Discard** and **Cancel**. **Save** writes every modified document. Save failures retain the modified markers and prevent closing. Closing a resource window keeps its unsaved data until the project closes.

## File explorer and reference tree

File Explorer browses `Assets` and `Data` through the source sidebar and breadcrumbs. Up stops at the selected root. The last valid browsing directory is restored, defaulting to `Assets`.

Right-click an entry for file operations or empty space for the current directory menu. Paste targets the current browsing directory.

Right-click a file or folder and choose **Show in File Explorer** on Windows or **Show in Finder** on macOS to open its containing directory and select it. This also works in expanded folders and search results. With multiple entries selected, it reveals only the right-clicked entry. The action is disabled for entries that do not yet exist on disk and does not save pending changes.

In list view, folder arrows expand or collapse nested folders in place; double-click a folder to enter it. `Right` expands a folder or selects its first child; `Left` collapses it or selects its parent. Expansion is remembered for the project session. Icon view and search results remain flat.

Search matches file names in the current directory and its subdirectories, ignoring case. Results include unsaved resources and display relative paths. Clearing the field restores browsing; changing directories or locating a file clears the search. Symbolic-link folders are excluded from expansion and recursive search.

Use `Ctrl/Command` with the mouse wheel or the bottom-right slider to scale icons and text from 50% to 200%. Press F5 to refresh external file changes.

Image and video entries show thumbnails when the format is supported. Selecting a Blueprint JSON file in a file selector previews its current appearance and animation, including unsaved changes; a missing appearance or texture displays the file icon.

Select an image, audio or video file in File Explorer and press **Space** to preview it. File selectors also preview audio and video in their right-hand pane. Playback starts paused; use the playback, seeking and volume controls, or **Escape** to close the preview or cancel selection.

Media previews support common audio and video formats, subject to the system’s codecs. Windows requires Microsoft Edge WebView2 Runtime. Previewing does not require the project’s FFmpeg option or a native game build, and files stay on your machine. Unsupported or damaged files display an error.

The reference tree shows which resources a file uses and which files use it. Create, rename and move managed resources through the editor to update recognised references. Arbitrary strings and references in source code must be updated manually.

Creating or copying a managed resource leaves it unsaved and adds no Undo step for the creation. A rename appears immediately in the editor. Global Save then writes the new paths and the updated references together. Deletion requires every recognised reference to be removed and saved first. Confirmed deletion is immediate and cannot be undone.

Copy/paste name conflicts produce names such as `name_copy.ext`, then `name_copy2.ext`, without overwriting existing files or folders.

The open menu at the upper right always offers the system file manager, which opens the current browsing directory. Selecting an entry saves it as the preferred open target. If it is unavailable in another project or on the current machine, the button uses the system file manager while retaining the saved preference. It lists VS Code or Cursor only when the corresponding application is installed. C++ Source projects also list an installed CLion, and Visual Studio 2022 on Windows. VS Code, Cursor and CLion open the project root regardless of the directory displayed in the file explorer. When the local `.idea` or `.vs` configuration is absent, opening CLion or Visual Studio for the first time prompts before running the project-provided environment generator. Cancelling leaves the project unchanged. Visual Studio opens the generated `Main.sln` at the project root.

## Console and performance monitor

The Console collects plug-in, build and runtime output. Input can be sent only while a compatible runtime connection is ready. **Edit → Development Tools and Settings → Performance Monitor** displays recent frame, logic and memory samples while the game is running.

### World-streaming samples

When profiling a composite world, the Performance Monitor includes an optional `worldStreaming` snapshot. Ordinary-map and unprofiled ticks do not include it.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `queueDepth` | Child regions waiting in the streaming queue. |
| `reading` | Regions currently in `Reading`. |
| `prepared` | Loaded regions in `Prepared`. |
| `active` | Regions in `Active`. |
| `dormant` | Loaded regions in `Dormant`. |
| `cacheBytes` | Conservative estimate used by the non-Active region cache. It is not exact process, Lua, native or GPU memory. |
| `publishMilliseconds` | Time spent converting and publishing regions during the logic tick. |
| `visibleTileChunks` | Unique 32×32-cell TileLayer chunks submitted by visible child layers in the latest draw. |
| `activeActors` | Actors currently present in the world's Active update/render batches. |

![Console output after a Game project run](../../../images/editor/console-output.png)

*The Console records launch progress, runtime diagnostics and the final process result.*

![Performance Monitor waiting for runtime telemetry](../../../images/editor/console-performance.png)

*A waiting monitor is normal when no compatible runtime session is active; the timeline fills after telemetry is connected.*

## Related pages

- [Common Particles](<Common Particles.md>)
- [Project Settings and Asset Layout](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md>)
- [Run, Debug and Package](<Run Debug and Package.md>)

documents.content:
# Project Settings and Asset Layout

A project stores editor and packaging settings in `Main.proj`, runtime settings in `Main.ini`, resources in `Assets`, authored data in `Data` and runtime code in `Scripts`. C++ Source projects also include the native sources described in [Build and Module Layout](<../Native C++ Development/Build and Module Layout.md>).

## Main.proj

`Main.proj` describes editor and packaging capabilities. The Game project enables the C++ runtime and FFmpeg and stores the preferred run-window mode:

```json
{
  "version": "v1.0",
  "Cpp": true,
  "ffmpeg": true,
  "IndividualWindow": true,
  "packaging": {
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "dev": false
  },
  "lastFileExplorerPath": "Assets"
}
```

The required top-level `version` is the engine compatibility version, written as `v<major>.<minor>`. For example, editor `1.0.7` creates `"v1.0"` projects. This edition supports `v1.0`. A missing, malformed or unsupported version prevents the project from opening. Opening a supported older project does not migrate its contents or change its version.

`packaging.version` independently stores the **game's** base release version, and `packaging.dev` selects internal test packages. Missing packaging values default to `"1.0.0"` and `false`; these defaults do not apply to the required top-level project version. Use Pack Options to save packaging settings, or override them for one command-line invocation; see [Release version and internal packages](<Run Debug and Package.md#release-version-and-internal-packages>).

Treat unknown keys as editor-owned state and preserve them. Choose the FFmpeg template to match the `ffmpeg` setting.

`lastFileExplorerPath` stores the last browsed directory relative to the project root. New Project initialises it to `Assets` for every template.

The editor stores the last selected map key in `lastOpenedMapKey` and saves it immediately when the editing selection changes, without saving map content. Reopening the project restores that map, including world maps and their child maps. Missing or invalid records select the first available entry; an empty project has no selection. Live-debug map changes do not overwrite this preference.

Editor appearance and tool preferences are shared through `Ludork.ini`, independently of this project workspace state. See [Global editor preferences](<Start Page Workspace and Shortcuts.md#global-editor-preferences>).

## Main.ini

Open **Game → Game Config** (`F3`) to edit the game’s language, display and audio settings in `Main.ini`. The entry script is shown read-only.

The language list uses the exported `Scripts/Source/Locale/*.lua` files, excluding `Core.lua`, and refreshes whenever Game Config opens. The current configured language remains available even if its export is missing. Export workbook changes before selecting a newly added language.

**Confirm** saves immediately; **Cancel** keeps the previous values. A failed write leaves the dialog open with an error. These settings are outside document Undo and unsaved changes.

![Game Config with display and audio settings](../../../images/editor/game-config.png)

*Game Config contains the language, display and audio settings.*

Game Config always shows Scale in the editor. The in-game Config window shows that row only when `Display.isDisplayScaleConfigurable()` reports that the host supports display scaling.

Editor runs use the project copy of `Main.ini`. A packaged Windows desktop game writes `Main.ini` and `Save/` into its runtime root, beside `Assets`, `Data` and `Scripts`, because Windows resolves user data to the process working directory. macOS and Linux desktop builds use `$HOME/<AppName>`, iOS uses `~/Library/Application Support/<AppName>`, and HarmonyOS and Android use the app-private user-data root. See [Game Settings Reference](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/Game Settings Reference.md>) for the keys, choices, defaults and application timing.

## System Config

Open **Database → System Config** (`F4`) to edit the configuration files under `Data/Configs`. The left-hand list shows each configuration by its relative key; selecting an entry such as **Audio** or **System** displays only that configuration's fields on the right.

Configuration files use JSON objects with `type: "system"` or no `type`. Their keys are paths relative to `Data/Configs`, without the extension.

Switching configurations keeps pending edits and does not save automatically. An asterisk in the list and window title marks changes. Use Ctrl+S on Windows or Command+S on macOS for global Save; Undo/Redo applies to the configuration selected in the list.

![System Config with a configuration list on the left and the selected form on the right](../../../images/editor/system-config.png)

*Select System to edit the game's title, dimensions and startup settings, or Audio to edit sound and music resources.*

## Assets

Authoring files live under the physical `Assets` directory. Stored resources use exact-case `/Game/Assets/...` paths with `/` separators and file extensions. Paths such as `Assets/...`, category-relative paths, native absolute paths and traversal paths are invalid. `PathVars` marks a field as a validated canonical `/Game/Assets/...` reference, unless `PathRoot` selects `"Project"` files or `"Data"` documents. Config `base` only sets the picker root. `/Game` works through Ludork resource APIs, while Standard filesystem APIs and direct LuaSF file constructors use native paths.

Resource resolution rejects symbolic links, broken links and reparse points from the target through the project root. An inaccessible path is rejected. Path conversion and picker roots may name a file or directory that has not been created yet, provided the existing ancestors pass the same checks. Stored resource paths remain case-sensitive on every platform.

Keep the conventional first-level folders so that selectors can filter correctly: `Tilesets`, `Autotiles`, `Characters`, `Animations`, `Particles`, `Icons`, `Fonts`, `Musics`, `Sounds`, `Voices`, `Shaders`, `Panoramas`, `Transitions`, `System` and `Videos`. The `.ldpak` option archives the complete `Assets` tree as root `Assets.ldpak`, including ordinary files directly under `Assets`. Logical resource paths remain unchanged.

Moving an asset does not automatically repair every stored reference. Open its reference tree before moving or deleting it, then update the affected data manually.

## Data and Scripts

`Data/Subtitles` stores [video subtitle](<Video Subtitles.md>) JSON documents with `type: "subtitle"` and a `sections` array. References use project-relative `Data/Subtitles/...json` paths. These managed editor documents are packaged with Data, including encrypted data and `Data.ldpak`.

`Data/Particles` stores [Common Particle](<Common Particles.md>) definitions. A particle reference is its extensionless relative key; particle textures use complete logical paths, conventionally under `/Game/Assets/Particles`.

`Data` contains JSON authored by the editor, and `Data/Locale/Locale.xlsx` is the localisation workbook managed by Official Locale Tools. Declarative UI assets live under `Data/UI/Assets`, while `Data/TextConfigs` holds shared or specialised text styles. Ordinary UI text styles are stored on their UI nodes.

`Scripts` contains runtime Lua, metadata and declarations. See [Lua Runtime and Modules](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md>) for module locations and ownership, and [Declarative UI Authoring Workflow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Authoring Workflow.md>) for UI assets and generated Views. [General Data and Text Config](<General Data and Text Config.md>) describes the files generated when saving project data.

Do not edit `Engine_meta.lua`, `GlobalCore_meta.lua`, `GlobalFunctions_meta.lua` or generated Core/LuaSF declarations by hand. Packaging removes `Scripts/stub` and rejects any misplaced `.d.lua`.

Keep `Data` and `Scripts` as loose directories while authoring. See [Run, Debug and Package](<Run Debug and Package.md#loose-and-packed-output>) for `.ldpak` output.

### Map and world-map assets

An ordinary map is `Data/Maps/<Name>.json`. A world is `Data/Maps/<WorldFolder>/` with exactly one `_world.json` and direct child-map `.json` files, and deeper nesting is not allowed. World loading reads only the direct `.json` files and ignores other regular files such as `.DS_Store`. The folder name is the world's path identity, while `_world.json` stores its independent `worldName`. Each direct child keeps its own editable `mapName`, so the file remains a complete map after it is moved out of the world, and the child file name remains its path and placement identity. The manifest is the world's selector and save identity, and it stays hidden in the Map List.

The manifest has this closed editor-owned shape:

```json
{
  "type": "worldMap",
  "worldName": "{WORLD_01}",
  "width": 256,
  "height": 192,
  "fog": {
    "enabled": false,
    "colour": [255, 255, 255, 255],
    "density": 0.5,
    "scale": 256,
    "velocity": [15, 15],
    "turbulence": 0.5,
    "seed": 0
  },
  "panorama": "",
  "layerOrder": ["floor", "default"],
  "placements": [
    {
      "map": "Map_01.json",
      "rect": [0, 0, 64, 64]
    }
  ]
}
```

`width`, `height` and `[x, y, width, height]` placement rects use zero-based cells. A rect must match the size of its child, and each child may appear once. Placements may touch, and uncovered cells are valid holes. Placements cannot extend beyond the world. The editor allows temporary overlaps while arranging maps, but rejects Save until they are resolved; saved manifests cannot contain overlapping placements.

`worldName` is a required non-empty display name. `layerOrder` is derived from the placed children and rejects contradictory cycles. The manifest owns the world display name, size, composition, global fog and global panorama, while audio, filters and ambient light remain child data.

Ordinary maps and worlds store fog in the same `fog` object. Configure its procedural world-space pattern through [Fog](<Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md#fog>); it does not reference an asset image.

## Limitations

Map renames and moves update recognised map-file settings and destinations in `GotoMap` and `RecordTelepoint` graph nodes. Arbitrary strings and dynamically constructed paths must be updated manually.

## Related pages

- [Project Templates](<../Getting Started/Project Templates.md>)
- [Lua Runtime and Modules](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md>)
- [Run, Debug and Package](<Run Debug and Package.md>)
