# Tilesets, Autotiles and Maps

## Tilesets and autotiles

Open **Database → Tilesets** (`F7`) to define a tileset image and its tile properties. Autotile data describes animated or connected tiles assembled from an autotile source. Keep images under `Assets/Tilesets` or `Assets/Autotiles`, and store the JSON definitions under the corresponding `Data` directory.

The window separates ordinary definitions and autotiles into the **Tilesets Data** and **AutoTiles** tabs. Select a definition from the list and edit its name. Then use the browse button beside **File Name** to choose its source image from the corresponding asset directory.

The map palette labels tileset tabs with `name`, while the JSON file name is the internal key. Changing the display name leaves references unchanged. Renaming the key updates every affected map's `layerTileset`, including unopened maps, following the shared [save and Undo rules](<Start Page Workspace and Shortcuts.md#editing-and-saving>).

![Tilesets Data tab showing per-tile passability](../../../images/editor/tilesets-data.png)

*In Passable mode, a circle marks a passable tile and a cross marks a blocked tile.*

![AutoTiles tab showing whole-asset passability](../../../images/editor/auto-tile.png)

*Autotile properties apply to the complete source rather than to each displayed source cell.*

Changing a tileset definition after maps have been authored can change what existing tile indices display.

Map JSON requires a `layerOrder` string array, which is the authoritative draw and Actor-processing sequence. `layers` and `actors` remain dictionaries keyed by those names, and the editor keeps the array synchronised. Runtime loading rejects missing, duplicate or unlisted layers. It never infers order from JSON object keys.

An ordinary tileset provides the **Passable**, **Material** and **Dir4** modes. Left-click toggles one tile's passability, opens its material editor or toggles the direction nearest the clicked edge. Shift+left-drag copies the pressed source tile's property through every crossed cell. The current mode chooses the copied value: Passable copies the boolean, Material deep-copies the complete material, and Dir4 copies all four directions. One drag is one Undo step. Autotiles provide **Passable** and **Material** for the whole asset and do not support this batch brush.

![Tile palette and layer list in the map editor](../../../images/editor/tile-layers.png)

*Use the tile palette together with the active layer; the selected layer receives every paint operation.*

## Map list and composite worlds

The Map List contains ordinary maps and worlds. A world row displays the `worldName` from `_world.json`. Expanding the row shows direct children by their editable `mapName`, while `_world.json` stays hidden. **World Map Properties** edits the world display name, whereas **Rename World Map** changes the folder and the runtime paths. A child keeps the ordinary **Map Name** field, so its file remains usable as a standalone map. Selecting a world opens its composition panel, and the context menus create each asset type. Copying a child assigns fresh Actor map tags without placing the copy.

Drag an unplaced child onto the world canvas, and drag a placed child to move it. Delete, Backspace or the context menu of the placement removes it. Each placement edit is one Undo/Redo step. Placements may temporarily overlap while editing, including when resizing a child map, but Save fails until all overlaps are resolved. Bounds and layer-order violations are still rejected during editing.

The selected placement is drawn above the others within each layer and takes priority when clicking an overlap, so it can be dragged away again. Without a selected placement under the pointer, the last placement takes priority. An obscured child can also be moved by dragging it from the child-map list onto the canvas.

![World composition panel with child-map thumbnails and placed maps](../../../images/editor/world-map.png)

*Child-map thumbnails show placement coordinates; the canvas previews how the maps fit together.*

The canvas and thumbnails appear as child maps load. A missing or unreadable child does not prevent the others from appearing. Editing maps or changing images updates their previews.

Scroll or pan the canvas. Use Ctrl+wheel on Windows/Linux or Command+wheel/pinch on macOS to zoom. The world canvas shares the game renderer with ordinary maps, including animated tiles and Actors, materials, layer shaders, lighting, fog and panorama. Child-map thumbnails use the same renderer at time zero. Only children needed for the visible area and its lighting are loaded for the canvas.

Resizing cannot place a child outside the world. Before deleting a placed child file, remove its placement and save. Non-JSON regular files are ignored, and Actor tags must be unique across the world.

A rename updates the recognised references listed in [Project Settings and Asset Layout](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md>). The world manifest and its child maps have separate histories, and automatic reference, placement and layer-order corrections create Undo barriers. The file explorer preserves the `Data/Maps` hierarchy, so root maps, world folders and children cannot move between levels or worlds. Create and delete them through the Map List.

Creating an ordinary map or a world child pre-fills Map Properties from the most recently modified ordinary map or world child in the project. This includes dimensions, ambient light, BGM/BGS and their filters, fog and all its parameters, and panorama. The file name and map name receive new defaults. Current-session edits, including unsaved changes and Undo/Redo, take priority; when no map has been edited in the session, the source is chosen by file modification time. Opening or saving a map does not change the session's edit order. With no existing map, the standard defaults apply. These settings are independent copies, so changing the new map's defaults leaves the source map unchanged.

The Ambient Light button shows a colour swatch and its ARGB value; a checkerboard indicates transparency. Click it to choose a colour.

Use the browse button beside BGM, BGS or panorama and select **Clear** to remove the file reference. World Map Properties uses the same selector for panorama. Confirm the properties dialog to apply the change.

Map Properties also selects an optional **Panorama** image from `Assets/Panoramas`. The runtime Cover-scales that image to fill `GameMap.MapViewRect`, then crops any overflow using the Camera's position as a fraction of the map's scrollable range. The left edge of the map shows the left of the panorama, and the right edge shows the right. An axis that cannot scroll uses the centre of that overflow. Ambient light tints the image, and point lights do not. A blank path disables the panorama. A world manifest may set a global panorama that covers the world Camera, while a child's `panorama` applies only when that child is loaded as a standalone map.

## Viewport

The small dropdown button at the upper left of the ordinary-map or world canvas opens **Viewport Options**. **View Mode** starts at **Unlit**: textures, materials and shaders keep their appearance under neutral lighting. Choose **Lit** to preview ambient light, Actor lights and their occlusion with the game renderer.

**Realtime**, **Show Fog**, **Show Panorama** and **Show Actor Origins** start enabled. Realtime advances preview animations and fog; disabling it freezes preview time while edits still refresh the image. **Show Light Bounds** starts disabled and is available only in Unlit. It displays read-only ranges with a black outline, white dashes, a faint light-coloured fill and a contrasting centre marker, without changing Actor selection or editing gestures. Origins and ranges are editor overlays and do not appear in thumbnails.

View Mode, fog and panorama choices also apply to child-map thumbnails, which remain at time zero. All six viewport options are shared within the project and saved immediately in `Main.proj` under `editor.mapViewport`. Reopening the project restores them; they do not change map data or create Undo steps. Previewing resolves the current map and Blueprint data without running gameplay scripts, constructors or Actor lifecycle callbacks. Hidden views stop requesting frames. If the native preview runtime is unavailable, the viewport shows its status; see [Construct, Export and Play](<Run Debug and Package.md#construct-export-and-play>).

### Fog

Map Properties and World Map Properties provide the same **Fog** settings. Enable fog to reveal its controls. The GPU generates the fog pattern in world coordinates; no fog image is required. Panning or zooming does not attach the pattern to the screen. A world can combine its global fog with fog inside each child region, using the same world coordinates across region boundaries.

| Setting | Meaning | Standard default |
|---|---|---|
| Enabled | Store whether the map renders fog. | Off |
| Colour | RGBA tint and alpha. | White, fully opaque |
| Density | Fog coverage from 0 to 1. | 0.5 |
| Scale | Pattern size in map pixels. | 256 |
| Velocity X / Y | Pattern movement in map pixels per second. | 15 / 15 |
| Turbulence | Pattern variation from 0 to 1. | 0.5 |
| Seed | Non-negative integer selecting a repeatable pattern. | 0 |

Lit uses scene lighting for the fog; Unlit uses neutral illumination. **Show Fog** only controls its editor preview and leaves the authored settings unchanged. Fog is saved as the `fog` object shown in [Map and world-map assets](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md#map-and-world-map-assets>).

## Layers and painting

Tile mode supports layer creation, rename, reorder, copy, paste and deletion. A layer may have a shader. Selecting a tileset tab changes the active layer's tileset immediately, and its existing tile indices are then interpreted against that tileset. Select a tile or autotile in the palette, paint on the active layer, and use erase for removal. Zoom and pan do not alter map data.

Each layer tab shows its name on the left and its visibility control on the right. Visibility is authored map data, so hidden layers are not rendered and are read-only. Layers and their Actors are drawn in the map's layer order. **Overview** shows all visible layers; selecting a layer dims the others without changing their stacking order.

The map uses one tile brush. Left-drag paints the selected tile or autotile continuously, Shift+left-drag paints a filled rectangle, and right-click samples the clicked cell. Alt+left-click (Option+left-click on macOS) fills the four-directionally connected region matching the clicked tile and autotile values. A multi-tile selection repeats from the clicked cell across that region; autotile selection and erase use the same fill shortcut. One brush stroke, rectangle or fill is recorded as one map edit for Undo. Hidden layers reject every editing route and show read-only feedback.

Saving during a stroke starts a new Undo step for subsequent movement. Undo and Redo end the active stroke, and pressing again resumes painting.

## Lights and actors

For Blueprint light defaults and component fields, see [Light Component](<Actor Components/Light.md>).

Use Actor mode to place a Blueprint instance, move it and edit its exposed attributes. The selected instance may override class defaults without changing the Blueprint itself. Add lighting through the Actor's `lightComp`; select the Actor normally and edit the component in **Actor Info**. Maps do not contain separate fixed-light objects or a Light editing mode.

In project editing, hold Ctrl on Windows/Linux or Command on macOS while left-dragging an Actor to select it and adjust its translation continuously in map pixels, without changing its grid position. Alt/Option+left-drag adjusts only its origin in local coordinates, accounting for rotation and scale; translation stays unchanged, so the image moves opposite the drag. Alt/Option takes precedence when both modifiers are held. A transform with a zero scale axis cannot be used for origin dragging. These operations write the instance's `defaultTranslation` and `defaultOrigin` overrides.

Ctrl/Command+wheel, or Command+trackpad pinch on macOS, scales the selected Actor in Actor mode. Scaling writes `defaultScale`, preserving the ratio and signs of its axes, including zero axes. Each wheel unit multiplies the value by 1.1; pinch changes it continuously. With no eligible editable Actor, the gesture zooms the map instead. Pinching without modifiers still zooms the map. These property shortcuts do not apply in Live Debug.

In Actor mode, Alt/Option+wheel or Option+trackpad pinch adjusts the selected Actor's `defaultRotation` instance override. Positive wheel movement and pinching outward rotate clockwise; negative movement and pinching inward rotate counterclockwise. Each wheel unit adds 15 degrees, and each 0.1 pinch increment adds 18 degrees. Alt/Option takes precedence over Ctrl/Command for rotation. Without an eligible editable Actor, these gestures retain their viewport behaviour.

Each property drag is one Undo step. Consecutive wheel or pinch changes to the same property and selection are grouped. Changing selection, map, layer or mode ends the interaction; saving starts a new Undo step for subsequent changes.

Ordinary maps and world previews draw an Actor whose resolved `visible` value is `false` at 25% opacity, including inherited defaults and instance overrides. Texture alpha, material opacity and the 50% dimming of non-current layers on an ordinary map still multiply this opacity. Selection outlines and error markers stay clear, and the Actor remains selectable and movable. These invisible Actors contribute neither lighting nor light occlusion. Hidden layers remain invisible, while placement ghosts and missing-texture placeholders retain their normal appearance. This behaviour is an editor preview aid, and invisible Actors remain hidden at runtime.

![Actor editing mode](../../../images/editor/actor-mode.png)

*Actor mode edits a placed Blueprint instance without changing its class defaults.*

An Actor light uses `LightComponent.lightOffset` relative to the centre of the Actor's local bounds. The complete Actor transform is applied to the offset, so the emitter follows rotation and scale. For a wall-mounted torch, place the offset at the visible flame on the room side of the wall, because the renderer does not move an emitter to a nearby passable cell.

The editor also previews lights on Actors without a texture. Actor scaling changes the emitter position, while the circular range keeps its `lightRadius` in map pixels and scales only with the editor's zoom.

`Material.lightBlock` is an opacity in the inclusive range `[0, 1]` for one `CellSize` of penetration. `0` is fully transmissive, `1` blocks direct light completely, and intermediate values compound by physical path length. For example, a value of `0.5` transmits approximately `0.707`, `0.5`, and `0.25` through half, one and two cells respectively.

An emitting Actor is excluded only from the dynamic occluders of its own light. It still blocks every other light, while tiles and other Actors at the same position remain occluders. Do not combine a wall and its torch emitter into one Actor. Use a wall occluder Actor and a separate torch Actor, because excluding the emitter also excludes the wall.

### Map tags in a world

Creating or pasting an Actor in a world child prefixes its default tag with the child file stem, and the editor enforces uniqueness across the world. Renaming a child or a world does not rewrite existing or custom tags. Copying a child rewrites the copied tags to `<new-child-stem>.<old-tag-body>` and updates their matching `BPClassVarChanged` keys.

## Map targets

The `startMap` file field and the Blueprint Transfer picker use the same map tree. Selecting a world stores `<WorldFolder>/_world.json`, and its position is a world-cell coordinate. Selecting a placed child stores `<WorldFolder>/<ChildFile>.json`, and its position is local to that child and is converted to world coordinates at runtime. Unplaced children remain visible in the tree but cannot be selected as runtime destinations.

## Live Debug

With **Individual Window** Play and [Live Debug](<Run Debug and Package.md#live-debug>) enabled, this panel shows the player's current ordinary map or world child. Allowed tile and Actor operations, and the save boundary, are on that page.

## Limitations

Arbitrary strings, custom protocols and dynamically constructed paths are not rewritten. Moving a tileset likewise does not repair gameplay strings.

## Related pages

- [Project Settings and Asset Layout](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md>)
- [Run, Debug and Package](<Run Debug and Package.md>)
- [Blueprints, Common Functions and Actors](<Blueprints Common Functions and Actors.md>)
- [New Game, Title and Scene Flow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/New Game Title and Scene Flow.md>)
- [Official Random Map](<../Plug-in Development and Installation/Official Plug-ins/Random Map.md>)

# Blueprints, Common Functions and Actors

A Blueprint is a JSON class definition beneath `Data/Blueprints`. It selects a native or Lua parent, stores editable attributes and, in graph mode, contains event graphs. Actor instances placed on maps refer to these classes.

## Create a Blueprint

Use **Game → New Blueprint**, or the equivalent command in the file explorer. Choose a parent that ultimately inherits `BPBase`, then choose a path beneath `Data/Blueprints`. Parent defaults and supported events are resolved from the inheritance chain. A new graph-mode Blueprint starts each inherited event with `Event → Parent`, including the event parameter connections.

A Blueprint key is its case-preserving path relative to `Data/Blueprints`, with `/` separators and no `.json` extension, such as `Actors/Guard`. Its class reference is `Data.Blueprints.Actors.Guard`. Key inputs accept an optional `.json` extension and normalise backslashes and surrounding whitespace. In a full class reference, every dot separates a module segment: `Data.Blueprints.Actors.json` refers to the key `Actors/json`.

## Class and instance values

Class attributes provide defaults for every instance, and a map Actor may override individual values. Components are declared by metadata and appear as structured fields. Hidden fields from `InvalidVars` are not ordinary editable properties.

The Blueprint editor resolves variable and component declarations through the complete inheritance chain. A child’s explicit value takes precedence over inherited defaults. See [Actor Components](<Actor Components/Overview.md>) for available components, adding and editing them, and instance overrides.

In the Blueprint editor and **Actor Info**, ordinary variables are grouped in grey dashed frames beneath the component list. Each frame names the class that first declared its fields, and hovering over the grey heading shows the full class reference. Inherited fields appear only in their original group, even when a child overrides their values. Fields contributed by a Script Mixin and custom Blueprint fields are attributed to the first Script Mixin or Blueprint that declares them.

When a Blueprint’s `ID` selects a General Data member, its `attributes` are shown read-only. Edit those values in General Data.

### Add a typed attribute

Use **Add Attribute** to enter a name, choose its type and set the initial value. For `enum`, choose an existing `Enums.*` module in **kind**, then select a key for the value. Lists and dictionaries also support enum items or values. A file field can constrain the asset selector with a base directory.

A new field saves its declaration in `attrDefs` and its initial value in `attrs`. If the name already belongs to an inherited field with no local value, the dialog fixes the type to that declaration and adds only an `attrs` override. Child Blueprints inherit the type and default; they cannot redeclare the inherited field. Removing an inherited override restores its inherited default. Deleting a field introduced by the current Blueprint removes both its declaration and local value, and is rejected while a descendant or map Actor override still depends on it.

Every saved attribute needs a declaration in metadata, an active Script Mixin or inherited/local `attrDefs`. An invalid declaration prevents the Blueprint from loading or being saved; the error names the Blueprint and attribute. Parent changes and field removal cannot leave descendants or map overrides with incompatible declarations. **Save Invalid Blueprint** permits unfinished graphs, but cannot bypass attribute errors. See [Blueprint attribute declarations](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Blueprint Scripting/Metadata Schema and Decorators.md#blueprint-attribute-declarations>) for the JSON format.

## Actor Library and Actor Info

The **Actor Library** lists Actor Blueprints in icon or list view. Select an entry for placement, or double-click it to open the Blueprint.

Filter by top-level folder and **All**, **Favourites** or **Recent** (the last 20 selected or placed Actors). Search matches names or Blueprint paths across all Actors, ignoring case; category and scope filters are disabled until the search is cleared.

Right-click an entry to open or locate its Blueprint, toggle its favourite state or remove it from Recent. Favourites are stored in `Main.proj` under `editor.actorFavorites`; they follow file moves and renames and are removed when the Blueprint is deleted.

In Actor mode, right-click an Actor on the map and choose **Locate Blueprint** to switch to File Explorer and select its Blueprint file. The action is disabled on empty space and for Actors without a Blueprint in the project.

For a selected map Actor, **Actor Info** shows its Blueprint reference with the **Open** and **Locate** actions, the grid position X/Y, the tag and the exposed class fields. Position and text edits merge into one Undo step for a continuous focused edit. A reset button beside an overridden field removes that instance override, and **Reset All** removes every class-field override for the instance and reveals the inherited Blueprint defaults again. When the Actor's layer is hidden, **Actor Info** stays available for inspection and Blueprint navigation, but its tag, position, reset actions and class fields are read-only.

Placing and deleting Actor instances can be undone in their map document. Deleting the Blueprint file itself is immediate and cannot be undone. If an instance was deleted and saved before its Blueprint was deleted, Undo cannot bring that instance back while the Blueprint is missing. Blueprint field changes, including Undo and Redo, refresh Actor visuals using the current inherited defaults.

## Graph mode

Enabling **Script Mixin** hides the entire right-hand graph and preview area, and the variables fill the available width. Disabling it restores that area and the previous column widths immediately. The same layout follows the inherited mode, Undo/Redo and reload, and existing graph data is retained.

Each Blueprint, Common Function and General Data graph has one built-in red **Event** entry, including events without parameters. Its execution output selects the start node by connecting to that node's execution input. Its data outputs provide the ordered event parameters. Reconnecting the execution output replaces the start; disconnecting it or deleting its target clears the start. Pure nodes have data pins only.

An unconnected entry is translucent and shows a persistent notice above it. A Blueprint says, “This event graph will not execute. An inherited implementation will be called if one exists.” Common Function and General Data graphs say, “This graph has no entry connection and will not execute.” Reconnecting the entry restores its normal appearance.

Use **New Event** to add a local graph. The name input offers inherited events that have no local graph; an existing local graph, even an empty one, cannot be added again. If the parent chain has the event, the new graph starts with a brown **Parent: Event Name** node connected to the entry and its parameters. This is one Undo operation. Opening an inherited event tab only displays it and does not initialise an override or modify saved data.

A Parent node is an ordinary editable node with execution input/output and one input per event parameter. Move, copy or delete it, change its parameter connections, or add it again from the node picker. Unconnected parameter inputs use their typed editors and defaults. Parent event nodes are available only in graph-mode class Blueprints. Add other nodes from the picker and connect compatible execution and data pins as needed.

An execution output pin holds one link, so connecting it again replaces the existing link, while an execution input pin accepts links from several nodes. A data output pin may fan out, and a data input pin holds one link. Right-click an editable node to disconnect every input or output link, copy or delete it; right-click empty canvas to add a node, paste, or organise the graph.

Right-click an editable node and choose **Convert to Plain Text Inputs** to replace all its editable parameter controls with text boxes. Connected inputs retain their usual display and pin types. Use **Restore Typed Inputs** to return to the type-specific controls. This works in Blueprint, Common Function and General Data graphs.

Plain text inputs still convert values to the parameter's declared type. String and file values preserve text; numeric and Boolean values become their corresponding literals. Containers, vectors and composite values use their existing JSON shape, including `$type`/`$value` for unions. Object and function inputs retain their existing expression semantics; this mode does not add expression support to numeric or other literal parameters. See [Metadata Schema and Decorators](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Blueprint Scripting/Metadata Schema and Decorators.md>) for stored shapes.

Invalid text remains visible as an unsaved draft with an error and does not replace the last valid parameter value. Correct it before restoring typed inputs or saving; **Save Invalid Blueprint** cannot bypass a draft error. Save errors identify the graph and parameter. The input mode and drafts survive graph switches and control refreshes only within the current editor window. Closing that window clears them; they are not written to the project or copied with nodes. New and copied nodes use typed inputs.

New, pasted and duplicated nodes are placed at the pointer, or at the viewport centre if the pointer is outside the graph. Duplicating a selection preserves its relative layout and internal links.

The primary modifier is `Ctrl` on Windows and `Command` on macOS.

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Ctrl/Command+N` | Open the node picker at the pointer position |
| `Ctrl/Command+A` | Select all editable nodes in the current graph |
| `Ctrl/Command+C` | Copy the selected nodes and their internal links |
| `Ctrl/Command+V` | Paste at the pointer position |
| `Ctrl/Command+D` | Duplicate the selection at the pointer position |
| `Arrow keys` | Move selected editable nodes by one graph unit |
| `Delete` | Delete selected editable nodes |
| `Ctrl+drag` on empty canvas | Box-select nodes; drag further to enclose more nodes, release to apply |

The built-in entry is virtual and automatically positioned, so it is excluded from select-all, manual movement, duplication and deletion. Parent call nodes remain editable. Graph shortcuts do not replace keyboard input while a parameter editor or another input control has focus, and mutating shortcuts are disabled for read-only graphs.

Common Functions provide reusable graphs. They are preferable to copying identical node sequences into many Blueprints.

General Data member graphs use the type’s event list, have no class attributes and cannot contain latent nodes. Their runtime behaviour is described in [General Data and Text Config](<General Data and Text Config.md>).

## Inheritance

A child Blueprint inherits fields and behaviour. Changing a saved parent path can alter inherited fields, events and compatible component data, so treat such a change with care. A Blueprint inheritance chain must use either graph mode or Script Mixin mode throughout; see [Script Mixin Authoring Workflow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Script Mixins/Authoring Workflow.md>).

## Related pages

- [Execution Flow, Events and Variables](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Blueprint Scripting/Execution Flow Events and Variables.md>)
- [Script Mixin Authoring Workflow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Script Mixins/Authoring Workflow.md>)
- [Tilesets, Autotiles and Maps](<Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md>)

documents.title: Overview
documents.content:
# Actor Components

## Purpose

Components add optional presentation or child-Actor behaviour to an Actor. Configure class defaults in a Blueprint and override them for individual map instances when needed.

## Applicability

| Component | Field | Available on | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Billboard](<Billboard.md>) | `billboardComp` | `Engine.Actor` and derived classes | Images and text above the Actor |
| [Light](<Light.md>) | `lightComp` | `Engine.Actor` and derived classes | A light that follows the Actor |
| [Emitter](<Emitter.md>) | `emitterComp` | `Engine.Actor` and derived classes | A Common Particle effect attached to the Actor |
| [ChildActor](<ChildActor.md>) | `childActorComp` | Default Gameplay `Source.MapActors.Enemy` and derived classes | A child Actor, used for the enemy damage readout |

The component list comes from the selected class's metadata and inheritance chain. `childActorComp` is declared by Enemy, not by the native Actor base; adding a component does not add a new field to an arbitrary class.

## Configuration

1. Open an Actor Blueprint to edit shared defaults, or select a placed Actor and open **Actor Info** to edit that instance.
2. In **Components**, use **+** to add an available optional component. Double-click an existing component to edit its fields. Follow the corresponding component page for its configuration.
3. Save the Blueprint or map document you edited.

A child Blueprint inherits an omitted value and uses its explicit value in preference to an ancestor's default. Optional components remain available even if no ancestor supplies a default; an unset component without a default is omitted from a new Blueprint's JSON. A map instance override takes precedence over its Blueprint defaults. In **Actor Info**, reset an overridden field to inherit again, or use **Reset All** to remove all class-field overrides for that instance.

## References

- [Blueprints, Common Functions and Actors](<../Blueprints Common Functions and Actors.md>)
- [Engine Actor and Component APIs](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Gameplay Types.md#component>)
- [Default Gameplay: Actors, Enemies, Items and Equipment](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/Actors Enemies Items and Equipment.md>)

documents.content:
# Billboard Component

## Purpose

Show a stack of images and text above an Actor when the player approaches, such as a name or interaction hint.

## Applicability

`Engine.Actor` and its derived classes expose `billboardComp`, an optional `Engine.BillboardComponent`. Configure it through the [component workflow](<Overview.md#configuration>).

## Configuration

1. Add or open `billboardComp` in **Components**.
2. Set `showRange`, the maximum player-to-Actor distance in map logical pixels; its default is `128`.
3. Use **+** and **-** in `items` to add and remove entries. Entries appear from top to bottom. Click **...** beside an entry's summary to edit it.
4. Choose `text` to set content, font size (default `12`) and colour. Choose `image` to select a picture through `path`; this editor label corresponds to the API's `image` field. Switching kinds preserves the hidden values.
5. Save the Blueprint or map.

## References

- [Actor Components](<Overview.md>)
- [BillboardComponent and BillboardItem API](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Gameplay Types.md#billboardcomponent>)

documents.title: Light
documents.content:
# Light Component

## Purpose

Attach a light to an Actor so its position follows the Actor's transform, for example a carried lamp or wall torch.

## Applicability

`Engine.Actor` and its derived classes expose `lightComp`, an optional `Engine.LightComponent`. Map lighting is authored through these Actor components, using the ordinary Actor selection and inspector.

## Configuration

1. Add or open `lightComp` through the [component workflow](<Overview.md#configuration>).
2. Set `lightColour` and a positive `lightRadius`. New components start with white light and a radius of `16`.
3. Set `lightOffset` from the centre of the Actor's local bounds to the intended light source; it defaults to `[0,0]` and follows the complete Actor transform. For a wall torch, use a separate Actor and place the light source on the room side of the wall.
4. Edit per-instance values in **Actor Info**, then save the Blueprint or map. Choose **Lit** in the viewport menu to see the result, or enable **Show Light Bounds** in Unlit to inspect the read-only range. See [Lights and actors](<../Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md#lights-and-actors>).

## References

- [Actor Components](<Overview.md>)
- [LightComponent API](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Gameplay Types.md#lightcomponent>)
- [Map light editing](<../Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md#lights-and-actors>)

documents.title: Emitter
documents.content:
# Emitter Component

## Purpose

Attach a Common Particle effect to an Actor, such as a flame, aura or sparks. Author the particle's tracks, textures and lifetime curves in the [Common Particle editor](<../Common Particles.md>).

## Applicability

`Engine.Actor` and its derived classes expose `emitterComp`, an optional `Engine.EmitterComponent`. For effects inside a UI, use `Engine.EmitterView` instead.

## Configuration

1. Create and preview a Common Particle resource under `Data/Particles`.
2. Add or open `emitterComp` through the [component workflow](<Overview.md#configuration>).
3. Select `resource` through the live `Enums.Particle` string enum, using its extensionless key such as `Combat/Hit`. An empty resource disables the effect.
4. Set `anchor` to a normalised point in the Actor's local bounds; it defaults to `[0.5,0.5]`. Adjust `offset`, `rotation` and `scale` relative to the Actor to position the effect.
5. Leave `beforeActor` false to draw immediately after the owner, or enable it to draw immediately before. Ordinary maps and composite worlds preserve their Actor-list and layer order; this setting does not introduce Y sorting.
6. Save the Blueprint or map.

## References

- [Actor Components](<Overview.md>)
- [Common Particles](<../Common Particles.md>)
- [EmitterComponent API](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Time Rendering and Particles.md#emittercomponent>)
- [EmitterView for UI](<../UI Controls in the Palette.md#engineemitterview>)

documents.title: ChildActor
documents.content:
# ChildActor Component

## Purpose

Create a child Actor from a class reference and place it relative to its owner. Default Gameplay uses it for the enemy damage readout.

## Applicability

Default Gameplay `Source.MapActors.Enemy` declares `childActorComp` as `Source.Components.ChildActorComponent`; Enemy Blueprints and their descendants inherit it. Native `Engine.Actor` does not declare this field, so it is not available on every Actor.

## Configuration

1. Open an Enemy Blueprint or select one of its map instances, then open `childActorComp` in **Components** using the [component workflow](<Overview.md#configuration>).
2. Set `className` to the full Actor class reference. Enemy defaults to `Source.MapActors.EnemyDamageText`; a Blueprint child uses a reference such as `Data.Blueprints.Actors.Guard`. An empty class name creates no child.
3. Set `relativePosition` for the child's local position relative to the owner; the default is `[0,0]`.
4. Save the Blueprint or map. Keep the default damage-readout class when that is the intended enemy behaviour.

## References

- [Actor Components](<Overview.md>)
- [ChildActorComponent API](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Source Classes/ChildActorComponent.md>)
- [Enemy API](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Source Classes/Enemy.md>)
- [EnemyDamageText API](<../../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Source Classes/EnemyDamageText.md>)

documents.title: General Data and Text Config
documents.path: docs/en_GB/Editor User Guide/General Data and Text Config.md
documents.content:
# General Data and Text Config

General Data is the editor-managed database beneath `Data/General`, suited to enemies, items, equipment, player presets, states and other data shared by many maps or Blueprints. Each JSON file defines a type schema and named members. Its Form, Table and member ability-graph windows share one document and one Undo/Redo history for that type file.

## Type structure

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `params` | Ordered field definitions with `type`, `defaultValue`, optional `comment`, and recursive type schemas for enums and containers |
| `members` | Named records that store values for those fields |
| `events` | Optional ordered event names; each member may store an independent graph for each one |

Supported fields include strings, booleans, integers, floating-point values, files, lists, dictionaries, `sf.Vector2f/i/u`, `sf.Vector3f/i/u`, `sf.Color` and `sf.IntRect`. New and edited fields save a complete recursive `type`, such as `{ "list": "int" }` or `{ "dict": "int", "key": { "enum": "Enums.GeneralData.Item", "valueType": "string" } }`. Existing `"type": "list"` with `itemType` and `"type": "dict"` with `valueType` remain readable. Enum, tuple and union composition follows [Metadata Schema and Decorators](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Blueprint Scripting/Metadata Schema and Decorators.md>). Select a union branch before entering its value.

In **Add Field** or **Edit Field**, select `enum`, choose its module through **kind**, and select an inferred or explicit scalar value type and a default value. Managed project enums use `string`. An empty source enum requires an explicit scalar type. For a dictionary, select its key type and key enum independently of its value type. These selectors write the schema itself; no separate `kind` or `reference` property is saved.

Use `{ "enum": "Enums.GeneralData.Item", "valueType": "string" }` for an Item key, `Enums.GeneralDataKey` for a type key, `Enums.Animation` for an animation key, and `Enums.Particle` for a particle key. Selectors include unsaved additions, renames and deletions. Lists, dictionary keys and values, tuples and unions support these enums.

Loading fails on a missing subtype, on a missing or unknown non-underscore member field, and on any value that does not match the schema. Use `any` for heterogeneous JSON values, because it preserves literal types and never evaluates strings.

`linkedType` is unsupported and rejected.

Each field definition may store an optional English `comment`. Enter it through **Comment** when adding or editing a field, and an empty comment is omitted. Form field names and Table headers show the comment on hover. This schema comment is distinct from a member value stored in a field that happens to be named `desc`, and it is plain project text rather than a locale key.

String enum selectors include **— None —**, stored as an empty string. Unknown nonempty values are retained; enums validate scalar types rather than option membership. Empty managed collections remain valid string enums. An enum-keyed dictionary row remains pending until a nonempty, unique key is chosen, so no placeholder key is saved. The old `GeneralDataVars` decorator and General Data field `reference` protocol are unsupported; express these choices in the type schema.

Enum declarations count as dependencies even when no member selects a value. Remove these dependencies before deleting a referenced type. Enum IDs preserve whitespace and quote characters literally.

Renaming a type automatically updates recognised module paths only where they are stored in editable JSON, including self references and other module names reassigned by identifier collisions. Dependencies declared in Lua metadata remain visible but do not trigger source rewriting. Animation and particle renames update typed scalar references. Dictionary key collisions reject a rename without partial changes, and Undo/Redo restores coordinated references under the shared [reference-update rules](<Start Page Workspace and Shortcuts.md#editing-and-saving>). Remove and save dependencies before deleting a referenced type. Ordinary strings and Lua or C++ source are not rewritten.

## Steps

1. Open **Database → General Data** (`F10`).
2. Select a type, or right-click the type-tab strip to create one.
3. Define fields before creating many members. Right-click a Form field name to edit its definition.
4. Add members and fill their values. Right-click a member in the list or a Table row to change its ID, duplicate it, remove it or open an available ability graph.
5. Manage type events from the type tab's context menu, then open member graphs with **Edit Ability Graph**. Event renames and deletions update all member graphs, and the runtime activates the graphs explicitly.
6. Inspect references before renaming or deleting types and members.
7. Save the data.

Save generates `Enums.GeneralDataKey`, each `Enums.GeneralData.<TypeName>` module, `Enums.Animation`, `Enums.Particle`, and `Source.Configs.GeneralDataTypes` with its LuaLS declaration. For example, `local Item = require("Enums.GeneralData.Item")` exposes `Item.EnemyBook`. Edit database records rather than these generated files. Type renames and deletions update their generated modules; handwritten files are retained.

Use `GeneralDataTypes.Create(typeName, memberID, memberData)` to restore a stored member with its ID and field types.

Editing a field can change its name, type, container item or value type, default and comment. Renaming preserves each member's current field value. Changing the field type, a list's item type or a dictionary's key or value type first asks for confirmation, then resets that field in every existing member to the new default value. Changing only the default does not overwrite existing members. Removing a field removes its meaning but does not automatically repair the scripts that read it.

Member graphs run synchronously through `Source.Gameplay.GeneralDataGraphAbility`, with `GameplayEventData` as their context. Use global nodes and that context; these graphs have no class inheritance, parent or self node. Only declared events are allowed, latent nodes are unavailable, and a missing start node returns `NoGraph`.

## Search and views

Search matches member IDs and direct scalar values such as names, numbers and booleans, ignoring case. It does not search inside containers or graphs. Each type retains its search, selection and Form/Table view while the window remains open.

Form edits one member in full. Table shows the ID and schema fields in declaration order, with direct editing for booleans, numbers and strings. For structured values, choose **Edit** to open that member in Form. Columns scroll horizontally. Editing follows the shared [Undo rules](<Start Page Workspace and Shortcuts.md#editing-and-saving>).

![General Data editor](../../../images/editor/general-data.png)

*Define the schema before entering records so every member uses the intended field types.*

## Game Variable Manager

Open **Database → Game Variables** (`F9`) to declare mutable values shared by Blueprint and the active game instance. The left side lists the declared variable names. Select one to edit its type, initial value and optional remark on the right, and the remark remains editor-only with no runtime effect. Variable names are runtime identifiers, so keep them stable once graphs, maps or scripts begin to reference them.

Use the search box to filter variable names case-insensitively. **New Variable** adds a declaration after asking for its name and type, and **Delete Variable** removes the selected declaration after confirmation.

![Game Variable Manager with a selected integer variable](../../../images/editor/game-variables.png)

*The selected declaration's type, initial value and editor-only remark are edited in the detail panel.*

Choose the type when creating a variable. The manager offers `bool`, `int`, `float`, `string`, `list` and `dict`, and these are written to metadata as `bool`, `int`, `float`, `string`, `any[]` and `Dict[string, any]` respectively. Lists and dictionaries use ordinary Lua tables, not the native `list` or `dict` of Standard. Changing an existing variable's type clears its initial value and replaces it with the empty default of the new type.

Save generates `Scripts/Source/Configs/GameVariables.lua` and `GameVariables_meta.lua` together. The first holds initial values and the second holds declarations. Edit variables through the manager, not these files; opening the manager alone writes nothing.

Blueprint fields or node parameters marked with `InstVar` use a searchable selector instead of a free-form text box. A corresponding `InstVarValue` field reads the type of the selected declaration and switches to the normal editor for that type. A type-filtered selector, such as the Game project conditional door, lists compatible variables only.

## Text Config

Ordinary UI text is styled on its UI node. Use **Game → New Text Config** for shared styles or named rich-text tags.

![Text Config editor](../../../images/editor/text-config.png)

*Text Config provides a focused editor for structured text data used by the project.*

Display strings such as `{ITEM_NAME}` are resolved when presented, not when data is loaded. See [Game Localisation Workflow](<../Plug-in Development and Installation/Official Plug-ins/Game Localisation Workflow.md>) for authoring and using localised text.

See the General Data Reference pages for the exact Game schemas.

## Limitations

Changing a schema or a game-variable declaration cannot automatically repair scripts, graphs, saves or string references. General Data and the generated game-variable declarations are project definition data, not stores for mutable play-session state.

## Related pages

- [Class](<General Data Reference/Class.md>) — the Game project Class schema
- [Blueprints, Common Functions and Actors](<Blueprints Common Functions and Actors.md>)
- [Game Localisation Workflow](<../Plug-in Development and Installation/Official Plug-ins/Game Localisation Workflow.md>)

documents.title: Animations and Curves
documents.content:
# Animations and Curves

## Animations

Open **Database → Animation Overview** (`F5`) to browse animation data. **Game → New Animation** creates a JSON asset beneath `Data/Animations`. The editor exposes the frames, timing, visual resources and event data of the animation format.

Keep source images under `Assets/Animations` or another intended asset folder. Non-empty image and sound entries store complete `/Game/Assets/...` paths.

![Animation editor showing frame timing and preview controls](../../../images/editor/animation.png)

*The animation editor provides frame editing and playback preview.*

### Exporting MP4 locally

Save the animation before exporting. From the repository root on Windows, run
`tools\animation_to_mp4.bat` to export all current `Game/Data/Animations` JSON
files to `Game/EditorCache/AnimationMp4`. Use `sh tools/animation_to_mp4.sh` on macOS.
The tool requires rebuilt ScriptTools with Pillow and a separate FFmpeg executable
with `libx264` and AAC; see [tool setup and options](https://github.com/JasonLeon01/Ludork/blob/main/tools/README.md#animation-mp4-export).

```bat
tools\animation_to_mp4.bat Game --input Game/Data/Animations/attack.json --output Game/EditorCache/attack.mp4
```

Exports retain frame rate, track order, position/rotation/scale interpolation,
horizontal flips and sound timing/trimming. Each video plays once through the
last image or sound segment, rounded up to whole frames. After visual segments
end, only the background remains. The canvas automatically fits all sampled
frames around the animation origin; `--size 512x512` fixes an even-sized canvas
and crops overflowing content without rescaling. MP4 uses an opaque background:
black by default, or `--background "#202020"`. `--mute` removes audio without
shortening the timeline, and `--overwrite` replaces existing output after a
successful export. Directory inputs are recursive and retain their subdirectories.
Time tags are not encoded as video events. Inputs are saved source JSON and loose
assets, not compressed animation caches or `.ldpak` packages.

## Curves

**Game → New Curve** creates a curve beneath `Data/Curves`. A curve has a name, a default value, pre/post infinity behaviour and ordered keys. Each key contains time, value, interpolation and arrive/leave tangents.

Use the curve editor to add, move and remove keys. Keep key times ordered. Avoid duplicate times unless the intended interpolation explicitly supports the discontinuity.

![Curve editor showing ordered keys and interpolation](../../../images/editor/curve.png)

*The curve editor displays keys and interpolation.*

## Referencing data

Metadata-driven selectors can reference animation and curve keys from Blueprints or General Data. Renaming the JSON file changes the logical key derived from its path, so inspect the reference tree first.

## Related pages

- [Common Particles](<Common Particles.md>) — GPU emitter tracks, atlas playback and normalised lifetime curves.
- [Project Settings and Asset Layout](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md>)
- [Execution Flow, Events and Variables](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Blueprint Scripting/Execution Flow Events and Variables.md>)

documents.title: UI Asset Editor
documents.content:
# UI Asset Editor

The UI Asset Editor lays out a declarative UI asset visually, with the Palette, Hierarchy, Designer, Inspector and Timeline in one window. Use it for any screen, window or reusable part that is authored by hand rather than built entirely from code.

## Open or create an asset

Choose **Game → New UI Asset**, or create and open the JSON asset beneath `Data/UI/Assets` through the project file explorer. Asset ownership (`Parts/<Owner>` versus `Shared`) is described in [Declarative UI Authoring Workflow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Authoring Workflow.md>).

![UI Asset Editor showing Palette, Hierarchy, Designer and Inspector](../../../images/editor/ui-asset-editor.png)

*The UI Asset Editor separates available controls, tree structure, visual placement and selected-node properties.*

## Steps

1. Set the design width and height for the asset.
2. Add a root control. A new screen normally starts with `Engine.Canvas`.
3. Drag system controls or exposed project assets from the Palette into the Hierarchy. [UI Controls in the Palette](<UI Controls in the Palette.md>) says what each control is for and helps you choose between them.
4. Select each node and edit control properties in the Inspector.
5. Configure the child Slot. Whether a container accepts children at all, and which Slot it supplies, is fixed by its `childPolicy` and `slotType`; the table is in [Children and Slots](<UI Controls in the Palette.md#children-and-slots>). Canvas children use anchors, offsets, alignment, auto-size and z-order, while List children use list-owned placement.
6. Give every node a meaningful name that is unique within the asset. Generated Views preserve these names as typed control or child-View keys.
7. Set **Exposed** only when the asset is a complete, reusable item intended to appear in the Project Palette.
8. Save, then use **Export** in the main window to generate the Lua View and declarations.

Drag a Palette control onto the middle of a container's Hierarchy row to add a child, or onto the top or bottom quarter of a row to insert a sibling. Dropping in blank Hierarchy space appends to the root. Double-clicking a Palette control also adds it using the current selection.

Moving a node to a Canvas preserves its visual position and fixed dimensions; stretched axes follow the new parent’s available size. Rotation and scale are retained, so a differently transformed parent can change the result. Reordering within one parent preserves the Slot. Each reparenting or indent/outdent action is one Undo step.

A WrapBox has one child template. The Designer displays every repetition, but editing any repetition changes the same template. See [UI Controls in the Palette](<UI Controls in the Palette.md>) for control properties and child rules.

## Timeline

The Timeline lists animations on the left and starts with no selection, an empty detail area and the authored UI appearance. Right-click to add or delete a local animation, then select one to edit its name, target, duration, pivot, tracks and keys. Clicking blank list space clears the selection. Colour keys use integer RGBA components.

Use play, pause, stop and scrubbing to preview an animation without changing the saved Slot layout.

A nested project node lists the Global animations inherited from its asset. Use the override action to create a same-name animation targeted at this instance, and then edit it locally, because inherited definitions themselves remain read-only.

## Asset paths and node names

The asset identity is the exact-case path relative to `Data/UI/Assets`, with forward slashes and no extension. Moving or renaming an asset rewrites managed JSON nesting references. The next Export regenerates its View and declarations, so update handwritten `require` paths and references to renamed nodes before exporting. The full key contract is in [UI Asset Schema and Control Registry](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Asset Schema and Control Registry.md>).

## Preview behaviour

After changing C++ UI code, use **Construct** before previewing it. Preview is unavailable while the native runtime is building. Use **Refresh Preview** to display pending edits.

The Designer displays the asset without running its Lua Controller. Include representative placeholder content and use `previewText` for text that code supplies at runtime. The `editor` data is used only for design.

Nested project assets cannot be expanded or edited from their parent. Open the original asset to change its contents.

See the [WrapBox API](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#wrapbox>) to access repeated instances.

## Related pages

- [UI Controls in the Palette](<UI Controls in the Palette.md>)
- [Declarative UI Authoring Workflow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Authoring Workflow.md>)
- [Declarative UI Controller Examples](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Controller Examples.md>)
- [UI Asset Schema and Control Registry](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Asset Schema and Control Registry.md>)
