documents.content:
# UI Controls in the Palette

The Palette lists everything you can drag into a UI asset: the engine's built-in controls, followed by the project's own exposed assets. This page covers the built-in controls — what each one is for, whether it accepts children, which Slot its children use, and which properties matter first. Runtime APIs are linked from each entry instead of being repeated here.

## How to read this page

Every entry is headed by the control's `controlId`, which is the exact value written into a node's `controlId` field. Entries are grouped by the Palette's own categories, and each carries one table:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Category | The Palette group the control appears under. |
| Children | `childPolicy` — whether the control accepts child nodes, and how many. |
| Slot | `slotType` — the kind of Slot this control supplies to each child. |
| Key properties | The control's own serialised properties, excluding those every control shares. |

### Children and Slots

`childPolicy` and `slotType` define which children a container accepts and how they are laid out:

| childPolicy | slotType | Controls | What each child gets |
|---|---|---|---|
| `multiple` | `canvas` | Canvas | Anchors, offsets, alignment, auto-size and z-order |
| `multiple` | `list` | ListView, ScrollBox | List placement owned by the parent |
| `single` | `list` | WrapBox | List placement, for exactly one template child |
| `none` | — | The other 19 controls | Nothing; they accept no children |

A Canvas Slot positions the child's local bounds. A List Slot does not accept Canvas Slot fields. The full field contract is in [UI Asset Schema and Control Registry](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Asset Schema and Control Registry.md#slots-and-resource-keys>).

### Properties every control shares

`visible`, `rotation`, `scale` and `origin` are on all 23 controls and are left out of the entry tables.

Six text-bearing controls — PlainText, RichText, FunctionalPlainText, FunctionalRichText, TextBox and DropBox — also carry an editor-only `previewText`. The Designer shows it so the layout stays readable before a Controller supplies real strings. It lives in the node's `editor` object and is design-only.

### The inline text-style group

Seven controls carry the same inline text-style properties: `textConfig`, `font`, `characterSize`, `bold`, `italic`, `underlined`, `strikeThrough`, `slantAngle`, `fillColor`, `letterSpacing`, `lineSpacing`, `lineAlignment`, `outlineColor`, `outlineThickness`, the four `glow*` fields and the three `gradient*` fields. They are CheckBox, DropBox, FunctionalPlainText, GamepadHintBar, PlainText, TabView and TextBox. Their entries below say *text style* rather than repeating that list. When `textConfig` is non-empty, the editor disables the inline fields and the runtime uses the TextConfig.

RichText and FunctionalRichText take `textConfig` but none of the inline fields; they style named tags through the TextConfig.

### System controls and project assets

The 23 controls below are built in. The Palette also lists project UI assets with **Exposed** enabled (`palette.exposed = true`). Add these as reusable units; edit their internal contents in the original asset.

## Layout controls

Layout controls organise their children, and are the only controls that accept child nodes.

### Engine.Canvas

The free-positioning container, and the normal root of a new screen. Children are placed by their own Canvas Slots rather than flowed by the parent.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout | any number | canvas | `size` |

Canvas sets the coordinate space and stacking order of its contents. See [Engine: Runtime Values and Functional Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Runtime Values and Functional Controls.md#canvas>).

### Engine.ListView

A multi-child list that arranges children into rows and columns, and draws only the ones currently visible.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout | any number | list | `size`, `columns`, `defaultItemHeight`, `fixItemHeight` |

`columns` defaults to 1 and `defaultItemHeight` to 32; `fixItemHeight` keeps every row at that height. See [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#listview>).

### Engine.ScrollBox

A clipped, scrollable viewport for more content than fits on screen. The native control owns scrolling, the overflow indicators and the clipping.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout | any number | list | `size`, `windowSkin` |

An empty `windowSkin` loads the current system window skin. See [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#scrollbox>), which also covers the window-skin overflow indicators.

### Engine.WrapBox

Repeats one authored child template at equal spacing — status flames, an icon grid, cell backgrounds.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout | one template | list | `size`, `count`, `spacing` |

Items flow left to right and wrap at the available width. Editing repetitions is described in [UI Asset Editor](<UI Asset Editor.md>); runtime access is in [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#wrapbox>).

## Visual controls

Visual controls draw something and take no input. `ProgressBar` belongs to this group even though the value it displays changes at runtime.

### Engine.CharacterView

Renders frame-animated character and enemy sheets inside fixed bounds.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual | none | — | `size`, `texture`, `textureRect`, `characterScale`, `animatable`, `switchInterval`, `shader`, `hue`, `colour` |

`textureRect` selects the initial frame, and `characterScale` adjusts its size. Set `animatable` and a positive `switchInterval` to play equal-width horizontal frames. `shader` accepts a complete `/Game/Assets/Shaders/...` path or an empty string. See [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#characterview>).

### Engine.EmitterView

Shows a GPU particle emitter inside the UI.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual | none | — | `particle`, `size`, `anchor`, `autoPlay` |

`particle` is an extensionless key under `Data/Particles`. Choose the effect and set its size, anchor and automatic playback. See [Common Particles](<Common Particles.md>) for authoring, and [EmitterView](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Time Rendering and Particles.md#emitterview>) for playback from code.

### Engine.Image

A static picture, stretched or tiled.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual | none | — | `drawAs`, `texture`, `textureRect`, `colour` |

**Draw As** is an enum selector in the Inspector: **Image** stretches the picture, while **Tile** repeats its texture region to fill the layout area and crops a partial final tile. Global UI Scale scales the complete result either way. An optional `textureRect` defines the tile. See [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#image>).

### Engine.ProgressBar

A background layer with a fill revealed from left to right.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual | none | — | `size`, `progress`, `backgroundTexture`, `fillTexture`, `backgroundTextureRect`, `fillTextureRect`, `backgroundColor`, `fillColor` |

`progress` runs from 0 to 1; values outside that range are clamped and non-finite values become 0. Each texture defaults to empty for a solid-colour layer, and a non-empty value uses a canonical `/Game/Assets/...` path. The fill is cropped to the current progress rather than compressed into it. Colours tint their own layer, so `[255,255,255,255]` preserves image colours. See [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md#progressbar>).

### Engine.Rect

A rectangle drawn from a window skin — panels, frames and selection highlights.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual | none | — | `size`, `windowSkin`, `opacityCurve` |

`opacityCurve` is relative to `Data/Curves`, with no directory prefix or extension, and resolves to a scalar curve. A Button with an empty `texture` uses the current window skin's selection-Rect image. See [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#rect>).

### Engine.SolidRect

A rectangle filled with one colour, with an optional outline.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual | none | — | `size`, `fillColor`, `outlineColor`, `outlineThickness` |

`outlineThickness` defaults to 0 and `outlineColor` to fully transparent, so an unedited SolidRect is a plain fill. See [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md#solidrect>).

### Engine.Window

A skinned window frame — the standard background for dialogs, menus and message boxes.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual | none | — | `size`, `windowSkin`, `repeated`, `colour` |

`repeated` selects texture repetition for the background when true and stretching when false; borders always tile between the corners. `colour` is an RGBA tint defaulting to `[255,255,255,255]`, so set its alpha in JSON for a translucent frame. See [Engine: Text and Windows](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Text and Windows.md#window>).

## Input controls

Input controls accept focus and player input. Each one is a `FunctionalBase`, which accepts focus and input only while it and every `FunctionalBase` ancestor are active, and while it and every `ControlBase` ancestor are visible.

`FunctionalImage` is in this group rather than under Visual: it is an Image that also takes input.

### Engine.Button

A clickable button with hover and pressed tints and an optional gamepad binding.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `texture`, `textureRect`, `colour`, `hoverColour`, `pressedColour`, `gamepadButton`, `gamepadLongPress` |

An empty `texture` uses the current window skin's selection-Rect image. Default and custom backgrounds remain visible for every input device. The bound gamepad glyph is shown when `Engine.Input.getInputHintDevice()` selects Gamepad; size, global bounds, hit area and separate text controls stay unchanged. `gamepadButton` is a logical name such as `"X"` and defaults to empty; `gamepadLongPress` defaults to false. A Button accepts no children, so its label is a separate text control. See [Engine: Runtime Values and Functional Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Runtime Values and Functional Controls.md#button>).

### Engine.CheckBox

A two-state toggle that draws its own label and reports changes.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `size`, `checked`, `windowSkin`, *text style* |

The label uses the inline text-style group or a `textConfig`. `toggle()` flips the state from code, and `setOnCheckedChanged` receives the result. See [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md#checkbox>).

### Engine.DropBox

A collapsed single-choice list that opens into a popup.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `size`, `windowSkin`, *text style* |

Populate the options from the Controller with `setItems`; they are not saved as asset properties. See [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md#dropbox>) for selection and sound callbacks.

### Engine.FunctionalImage

An Image that also accepts focus and input, and the base of CharacterView.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `drawAs`, `texture`, `textureRect`, `colour` |

It serialises the same properties as Image and inherits its `drawAs` API. Choose Image when nothing needs to click the picture. See [Engine: Runtime Values and Functional Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Runtime Values and Functional Controls.md#functionalimage>).

### Engine.FunctionalPlainText

A PlainText that also accepts focus and input.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `text`, `colour`, *text style* |

See [Engine: Runtime Values and Functional Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Runtime Values and Functional Controls.md#functionalplaintext>).

### Engine.FunctionalRichText

A RichText that also accepts focus and input.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `textConfig`, `text`, `colour` |

See [Engine: Runtime Values and Functional Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Runtime Values and Functional Controls.md#functionalrichtext>).

### Engine.GamepadHintBar

Shows up to three gamepad hints, centred in its size.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `size`, *text style* |

The hints appear only while a gamepad is connected. The Controller supplies up to three `Engine.GamepadHint` entries. See [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md#gamepadhintbar>).

### Engine.Slider

A draggable numeric value within a range.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `size`, `minValue`, `maxValue`, `value`, `lineTexture`, `handleTexture` |

`minValue` and `maxValue` are integers defaulting to 0 and 100, and the two textures default to `/Game/Assets/System/SliderLine.png` and `/Game/Assets/System/SliderHandle.png`. Editing covers pointer, keyboard and touch input, and reports through `setOnValueChanged`. See [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md#slider>).

### Engine.TabView

A row of selectable tabs.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `size`, `windowSkin`, `items`, *text style* |

`items` is a construction-only, non-empty `string[]`. Assets normally use `#TAB 1...` placeholder values so the native preview shows each tab; before the first visible frame the Controller supplies localised labels and binds selection behaviour. `selectedIndex` and key-hint tables are runtime-only, and `tabCount` is not accepted. See [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md#tabview>).

### Engine.TextBox

An editable single-field text input.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | none | — | `size`, `windowSkin`, `text`, *text style* |

Set `text` for the initial runtime value; `previewText` affects the Designer only. See [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md#textbox>) for editing and callbacks.

## Text controls

Text controls draw strings and take no input. Use the Functional variants when the text itself must be focusable or clickable.

### Engine.PlainText

Static text styled directly on the node.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Text | none | — | `text`, `colour`, *text style* |

See [Engine: Text and Windows](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Text and Windows.md#plaintext>).

### Engine.RichText

Static text with named tag styles resolved through a TextConfig.

| Category | Children | Slot | Key properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| Text | none | — | `textConfig`, `text`, `colour` |

See [Engine: Text and Windows](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Text and Windows.md#richtext>).

## Choosing between controls

| To do this | Use |
|---|---|
| Position children freely, or start a new screen | Canvas |
| Flow children into rows and columns | ListView |
| Scroll content that does not fit | ScrollBox |
| Repeat one template at equal spacing | WrapBox |
| Show a picture, stretched or tiled | Image, or FunctionalImage when it must take input |
| Show an animated character or enemy sheet | CharacterView |
| Show a particle effect | EmitterView |
| Show progress from 0 to 1 | ProgressBar |
| Draw a skinned dialog frame | Window |
| Draw a skinned panel or selection highlight | Rect |
| Draw a solid-colour block | SolidRect |
| Show static text | PlainText, or RichText for named tag styles |
| Show text that must be focusable | FunctionalPlainText or FunctionalRichText |
| Accept a click | Button |
| Accept a yes/no choice | CheckBox |
| Accept one choice from a list | DropBox |
| Accept a number within a range | Slider |
| Accept typed text | TextBox |
| Switch between pages | TabView |
| Show gamepad button hints | GamepadHintBar |

## Runtime-only types

`Engine.SectorShape` and `Engine.AssetInstance` are available to code but are not built-in Palette controls. See the [interactive control reference](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md>) for their APIs. Exposed project assets appear in the Palette by their own names, and their generated View exposes the runtime asset through `.instance`.

## Related pages

- [UI Asset Editor](<UI Asset Editor.md>)
- [UI Asset Schema and Control Registry](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Asset Schema and Control Registry.md>)
- [Declarative UI Authoring Workflow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Declarative UI/Authoring Workflow.md>)
- [Engine: Layout and Image Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Layout and Image Controls.md>)
- [Engine: Interactive and Declarative UI Controls](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Interactive and Declarative UI Controls.md>)
- [Native UI Adapters](<../Native C++ Development/Native UI Adapters.md>)

documents.title: Common Particles
documents.content:
# Common Particles

Common Particle assets contain ordered GPU emitter tracks. Use them on an Actor through `EmitterComponent`, or in a UI through `Engine.EmitterView`.

## Author and preview

Choose **Game → New Common Particle** or create a particle in the project file explorer. **Database → Common Particle Overview** (`F6`) lists the resources under `Data/Particles`. Select a resource to edit its tracks, properties and lifetime curves. Right-click the track list to add a track; right-click a track to select it and enable Duplicate Track and Remove Track for that item. Those two actions are disabled when opening the menu on empty space. The preview can isolate the selected track. Track order also determines drawing order within an emitter.

![Common particle editor showing a resident-loop effect](../../../images/editor/common-particle-editor.png)

*The track list is on the left, the preview and lifetime curve are in the centre, and properties are on the right.*

The Texture Rect fields set the texture region’s position and size. Preview controls include Play/Pause, Stop, Restart, a single simulation step, time entry, seeking, playback speed and zoom. A step advances `1 / simulationRate` seconds. Seeking pauses playback and can take longer for later times; preview controls do not change the saved resource.

Resource edits follow the shared [save and Undo rules](<Start Page Workspace and Shortcuts.md#editing-and-saving>). After C++ changes, use **Construct** to update the preview. Missing resources or unsupported GPU capabilities display an error.

## Resource identity and schema

Store definitions in `Data/Particles/<key>.json`. References use the exact-case key with `/` separators and no directory prefix or extension, for example `Combat/Hit`. Textures use complete `/Game/Assets/...` logical paths. Definitions have no version field.

The following JSON format uses colour components in 0–255. For the corresponding runtime configuration types, see the [Emitter configuration API](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Time Rendering and Particles.md#emittertrack>).

```json
{
  "type": "particle",
  "simulationRate": 60,
  "seed": 1,
  "tracks": [
    {
      "name": "Glow",
      "mode": "resident",
      "capacity": 64,
      "count": 32,
      "loop": true,
      "shape": "disk",
      "radius": 24,
      "lifetime": [0.8, 1.6],
      "speed": [4, 12],
      "texture": "/Game/Assets/Particles/Glow.png",
      "blend": "add",
      "curves": {
        "alpha": {
          "keys": [
            { "time": 0, "value": 0 },
            { "time": 0.2, "value": 1 },
            { "time": 1, "value": 0 }
          ]
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

This example requires the named texture in the project. An empty texture is transparent. `simulationRate` is an integer from 1 to 240, default 60; `seed` is an integer from 0 to 16,777,215, default 1. `tracks` is an ordered array with unique track names. A fixed seed supports repeatable authoring on the same runtime and GPU; floating-point GPU simulation is not a cross-device determinism guarantee.

| Track fields | Default and meaning |
|---|---|
| `name`, `enabled` | `"Track"`, `true`; names identify tracks for manual emission. |
| `mode` | `"emission"` or `"resident"`; see the lifecycle rules below. |
| `duration`, `delay`, `loop`, `prewarm` | `2`, `0`, `true`, `false`; timing uses seconds. `duration` is positive and `delay` is non-negative. |
| `capacity`, `count` | `1024`, `min(32, capacity)`; capacity is 1–1,000,000, and resident count is 0–capacity. |
| `rate`, `distanceRate`, `bursts` | `30`, `0`, `[]`; particles per second, particles per logical pixel of host motion, and scheduled bursts. |
| `shape`, `extent`, `radius`, `innerRadius` | `"point"`, `[32,32]`, `16`, `8`; shapes are `point`, `line`, `rectangle`, `disk`, `ring`. A line uses `extent.x`; rectangles use both extents. Radii are non-negative, and a ring's inner radius cannot exceed its outer radius. |
| `direction`, `spread` | `-90`, `30` degrees; initial direction is sampled within `direction ± spread`. Positive Y points down. |
| `lifetime`, `speed` | `[1,2]` seconds, `[20,40]` logical pixels/second; arrays contain minimum and maximum values. Lifetime is positive. |
| `sizeMin`, `sizeMax` | `[8,8]`, `[16,16]` logical pixels; non-negative minimum/maximum size for each axis. |
| `rotation`, `angularVelocity` | `[0,360]` degrees, `[0,0]` degrees/second. |
| `colourMin`, `colourMax` | Both `[255,255,255,255]`; minimum/maximum RGBA components in 0–255. |
| `gravity`, `radialAcceleration`, `tangentialAcceleration`, `damping` | `[0,0]`, `0`, `0`, `0`; accelerations use logical pixels/second², and non-negative damping applies exponential velocity decay. |
| `texture`, `textureRect` | `""`, `[0,0,0,0]`; rectangle is integer `[x,y,width,height]`. Zero width and height select the entire image; otherwise it must be positive and inside the image. |
| `columns`, `rows`, `frameCount`, `frameRate` | `1`, `1`, `1`, `0`; grid dimensions are 1–4096, count is 1–`columns × rows`, and frame rate is non-negative frames/second. |
| `randomStartFrame`, `frameLoop` | `false`, `true`; frames run left-to-right, then top-to-bottom. Zero frame rate holds the initial frame. A non-looping sequence holds its last frame. |
| `space`, `scaleMode`, `blend` | `"local"`, `"hierarchy"`, `"alpha"`; alternatives are described below. Blend also accepts `"add"`. |
| `offset`, `rotationOffset`, `scale` | `[0,0]`, `0` degrees, `[1,1]`; the track's transform relative to its host. |
| `curves` | Optional lifetime channels `speed`, `sizeX`, `sizeY`, `rotation`, `red`, `green`, `blue`, `alpha`. |

Each burst is `{ "time": 0, "count": 16, "cycles": 1, "interval": 0 }`. Its first time is within `[0,duration)`, count is 0–1,000,000, cycles is 1–10,000, and interval is non-negative seconds, strictly positive for repeated bursts. Numeric inputs must be finite and minimum/maximum ranges ordered.

Curves accept an inline scalar [Curve](<Animations and Curves.md>) or an extensionless key under `Data/Curves`. Their key times use normalised particle age `[0,1]`. Speed, size and RGBA channels multiply their base values and default to 1; rotation adds degrees and defaults to 0. Inline curves support `defaultValue`, `preInfinity`, `postInfinity` and `keys` containing `time`, `value`, `interpolation`, `arriveTangent` and `leaveTangent`. The runtime samples each channel into a 256-entry GPU lookup table, so rendered curves are an approximation of the source curve.

## Emission, space and ownership

`emission` combines time emission, host-distance emission, bursts and `emit(trackName, count)`. `loop` repeats its duration; disabling it ends automatic emission after the duration while existing particles finish. Fixed GPU slots form a ring: births reuse the next slots and overwrite the oldest slots when capacity is exhausted. Capacity is a simulation budget, not a guarantee that every requested particle survives its full lifetime.

`resident` creates `count` particles after its delay. With `loop = true`, each particle repeats its own lifetime without further emission. With looping disabled, the initial set expires once. Time/distance emission, bursts and manual `emit` do not apply to resident tracks. Atlas animation is independent of this lifecycle mode.

`prewarm` applies only to looping tracks. Before normal playback, the GPU replays complete emission cycles covering the maximum particle lifetime with the host held at its current position. Work is limited to 120 fixed steps per frame. Public playback time remains zero while warming, and restarting repeats this process.

In `local` space, existing particles follow the current host transform. In `world` space, particles retain their birth position and transform after the host moves. For an Actor the domain is map coordinates; for an `EmitterView` it is its containing Canvas's logical coordinates. UI particles do not use the map View. Canvas scaling is applied once when composing the UI, and moving a view to another Canvas resets its particles because the coordinate domain changes.

`hierarchy` applies the full host and track scale to shape, motion and particle size. `local` scale mode removes host scale while retaining track scale. `shape` applies the combined scale only to the spawn shape, retaining unscaled particle size and motion.

To attach a particle resource to an Actor, follow [Emitter Component](<Actor Components/Emitter.md>). It covers resource selection, placement relative to the Actor and drawing order.

Add `Engine.EmitterView` as a visual UI node under an existing Canvas or List container, or construct it in code. Configure `particle`, `size`, `anchor` and `autoPlay`; `getEmitter()` returns its playback object. The UI node owns its normal layout and clipping through `ControlBase` and its parent. It does not require an Actor.

Particles pause while their Actor is invisible or dormant, or their UI is hidden or unmounted. Showing the owner resumes its state; movement while hidden does not produce distance-based emission. A manually paused emitter stays paused. Destroying the owner clears its particles, which are not included in map persistence.

See [Emitter, EmitterComponent and EmitterView APIs](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Time Rendering and Particles.md#emitter>) for playback controls and performance statistics.

## GPU requirements

Common Particles require a compatible GPU; mobile builds require OpenGL ES 3. Missing GPU capabilities produce an error, with no CPU fallback.

## Limitations

Collision, trails, noise and sub-emitters are outside this particle feature.

## Related pages

- [UI Controls in the Palette](<UI Controls in the Palette.md#engineemitterview>)
- [Project Settings and Asset Layout](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md>)
- [Resources, Audio, Video and Effects](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/Resources Audio Video and Effects.md>)
- [Engine: Time, Rendering and Particles](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Global and Core Modules/Core Modules/Engine/Time Rendering and Particles.md>)

documents.title: Video Subtitles
documents.content:
# Video Subtitles

Create a subtitle document in the project file explorer under `Data/Subtitles`, or double-click an existing subtitle JSON file to open its editor. Subdirectories are supported. Subtitle documents use the normal Save, Undo/Redo, unsaved-change and close-confirmation workflow.

## Edit and preview

The upper-left area previews the picture and subtitles, the upper-right area edits the selected section, and the timeline spans the bottom. Select a section by its array position; sections have no separate name or identifier.

![Subtitle Editor with video preview, multilingual text controls and timeline](../../../images/editor/subtitle-edit.png)

Add, select, delete or move sections on the timeline, and drag their edges to adjust their duration. Zoom the timeline and drag the playhead to inspect a time. The properties pane also accepts precise start and end times in seconds. Save orders sections by start time and rejects invalid times or overlapping sections.

Each section has a multilingual switch, off by default for new sections. Turning it on places the existing text under `en_GB` and adds the document's other languages with empty text. Turning it off retains the selected language, with confirmation before discarding other translations from that section.

All multilingual sections share the same language keys. Use `+` and `−` below the language list to add or delete a language throughout the document, or right-click a language to rename it. Names must be nonempty and unique; new languages start with empty text.

Within a section, all languages have the same number of text rows; different sections can have different counts. Click or focus a row, then use `↑`, `↓`, `+` and `−` below the text list to move it, append an empty row or delete it across that section's languages. Typing changes only the selected translation. Switching languages keeps the row selection; switching sections selects the first row. Empty text lists and language lists are allowed, with text operations disabled when no language exists.

When opening existing data, the editor combines the language keys and pads missing languages or shorter arrays to each section's longest array with empty strings, preserving existing text. This is one unsaved, undoable change. Undo restores the original data; padding runs again only with the next content edit and shares that edit's undo step.

Use Play/Pause, Stop, the current time and preview language to check timing. Without a reference video, playback uses a plain background and ends at the last section's end time. An empty subtitle document remains editable.

Choose a project video for temporary reference, or clear it to return to the plain background. Video preserves its aspect ratio and plays synchronised audio, with a mute control. Seeking pauses audio and restores the previous playback state when positioning finishes. Preview duration is the longer of the video and subtitle durations; after video ends, remaining subtitles appear on the plain background. A project without FFmpeg reports that it is not an FFmpeg project when a video is selected; subtitle editing and plain-background preview remain available.

The reference video, preview language, playhead and mute setting belong to the window session and are not saved in the subtitle document.

## Data format

Store UTF-8 JSON beneath `Data/Subtitles` and reference it with a project-relative, case-sensitive `Data/Subtitles/...json` path. Loose files and entries in `Data.ldpak` use the same paths. Encrypted `.ldc` data is resolved through the same `.json` reference. Paths must stay beneath `Data/Subtitles`; absolute paths and directory traversal are invalid. A subtitle document has `type: "subtitle"` and a `sections` array:

```json
{
  "type": "subtitle",
  "sections": [
    {
      "startTime": 0.5,
      "endTime": 3.0,
      "content": {
        "en_GB": ["Speaker 1's content", "Speaker 2's content"],
        "zh_CN": ["角色一的内容", "角色二的内容"]
      }
    },
    {
      "startTime": 3.0,
      "endTime": 5.5,
      "content": ["Content shared by all languages"]
    }
  ]
}
```

Times are finite numbers in seconds with `0 ≤ startTime < endTime`. A section is active from its start time, inclusive, to its end time, exclusive. Sections may touch but cannot overlap; gaps display no subtitles. An empty `sections` array is valid.

`content` is either a string array used directly or a dictionary of language keys to string arrays. The dictionary first selects the current game language, then `en_GB` if that key is missing. If neither exists, no subtitle is displayed. An existing empty array explicitly displays nothing and does not fall back.

## Playback and layout

Pass the subtitle path as the optional fourth argument of [Video.PlayVideo](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Node Functions/Video.md>). Missing or empty paths keep video-only playback. A specified resource must load and validate successfully; malformed subtitle documents report an error.

Subtitles follow the video's playback clock and disappear when playback ends or is skipped. The renderer uses the game's default font and size, with white text and a black outline. Strings appear from top to bottom in array order, wrap as needed and centre each visual line horizontally. The block sits at the bottom of the logical viewport, leaving 5% on each side and 3% below it. Content taller than the available area scales down uniformly to fit. Runtime playback and native editor preview share the subtitle layout.

## Related pages

- [GlobalFunctions.Video](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Node Functions/Video.md>)
- [Project Settings and Asset Layout](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md>)
- [Resources, Audio, Video and Effects](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/Resources Audio Video and Effects.md>)

documents.content:
# Run, Debug and Package

Run a project, edit its live state and package it for a supported platform.

## Construct, Export and Play

The toolbar orders its actions as **Construct → Export → Play**. Standalone projects hide Construct. **Construct** saves the project and builds the Debug executable and preview runtime without launching the game. Native binding generation remains part of the build; UI and locale export is a separate operation.

Ordinary-map, world and thumbnail previews use this native preview runtime. C++ Source projects prepare it through Construct; Standalone projects use the matching bundled runtime. A missing or incompatible runtime is reported in the viewport. Map previewing does not start gameplay and does not require Play or an Export after each map edit.

**Export** saves the project, runs Export plug-in hooks and generates UI Views, declarations and locale files. Export again after changing the inputs or removing generated files. A failed or cancelled export does not count as a successful export.

Variables and General Data still take effect on Save; their Lua files remain under version control and are outside Export. Ordinary Save, Construct, direct run and template creation do not generate UI files. The explicit `ui-assets generate` command produces UI files only; it does not run Export hooks or publish a complete editor export record.

Play is enabled after the first successful Export and, for C++ Source, a successful Debug build through **Construct** or `tools/build_cpp`. A bare CMake build does not enable Play.

Deleting `EditorCache` requires another Construct for C++ Source and another Export before Play.

After the first successful build and export, Play offers **Build and Play** or **Export and Play** when files have changed. Cancelling or failing either operation stops launch. Lua, UI JSON, game data and localisation edits do not require a native build.

While Play is preparing or running the game, its button becomes **Stop**. Clicking Stop cancels preparation or stops the current process. Construct and Export disable repeated actions and project editing until completion. Natural exit, cancellation and failures restore editing; closing the project cancels active preparation.

These operations keep the current tab selected; open **Console** manually to view output.

**Individual Window** opens a separate game window and keeps the selected map or world visible in the editor. Project editing, including already open document windows, Undo/Redo and editing shortcuts, is disabled during preparation, compilation and export. Running keeps these restrictions unless **Live Debug** was enabled before Play; see below. The Console, performance monitoring and Help remain available. Embedded mode instead displays the Windows runtime inside the editor and locks the game viewport layout. This window choice is configurable only on Windows; other platforms always use an individual window. An unavailable Windows embedded handle fails with `EmbeddedHandleUnavailable`.

Failures are reported in the operation dialog and Console. An export failure prevents Play or Pack from continuing; correct the first validation, hook or generation error and export again.

## Server connections

For a C++ Source project, configure the local development connection through **Game → Test Server Settings**, then rebuild Debug. **Pack Project → Enable Ludork Server** sets a separate Release connection and starts blank each time; dev packages also use Release. Standalone hides both options. See [Simple Server](<../Simple Server/Deployment and Editor Settings.md>) for deployment and connection settings.

## Live Debug

Enable **Edit → Development Tools and Settings → Live Debug** before Play to edit the running map from the editor. The project preference defaults to off and cannot change during preparation or running. It requires **Individual Window**; selecting embedded mode clears and disables it. Preparation, Construct and Export keep their normal editing locks.

Once the game is running, the editor follows the player's current ordinary map or the current child of a composite world. Manual map switching is disabled. World holes, maps that are still loading, scenes without a live player and an unavailable connection are read-only. **File Explorer** can browse and locate resources; creating, renaming, moving, deleting and editing project files remain disabled.

The native viewport reflects the live Actors' appearance, transforms, materials and lights, together with the map's fog, panorama and ambient light. A world child retains world coordinates for these effects. [Viewport Options](<Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md#viewport>), including Lit/Unlit, affect the editor image only; they do not change the running game or grant additional editing permissions.

On existing editable layers, Live Debug allows:

- The same tile brush as [project map editing](<Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md#layers-and-painting>): paint, erase, sample and fill. Layer structure, visibility, tileset assignment, map properties and world placements stay locked.
- Selecting and deleting live Actors, including the player, runtime-spawned Actors and child Actors, and moving top-level Actors. The editor cannot add, paste or duplicate Actors.
- Reading **Actor Info** and changing ordinary variables, including `Optional[T]` when `T` is supported. Optional values accept `nil`; non-nil values still require the declared type. **Components**, the parent class, Blueprint identity and map tags stay read-only.

Actor positions, creation, destruction and inspected values follow the running game. Moving an Actor cancels its current movement route. Deletion uses normal Actor destruction and its existing lifecycle callbacks. Hidden Actors remain inspectable according to the [map preview rules](<Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md#lights-and-actors>); hidden layers stay read-only. Live edits have no Undo/Redo and do not write project documents or mark them modified.

**World Outliner** nests child Actors under their current parents. Clicking or dragging a child on the map selects its top-level owner; dragging moves that owner and its descendants. Select a child in **World Outliner** to inspect or edit ordinary variables, or to delete it through its normal lifecycle. Direct child movement, including **Actor Info** coordinates, is disabled.

Edits belong to the live Actor or map instance. They remain while that instance exists, including a dormant world instance, and are not replayed onto rebuilt instances. Rebuilt instances use the project's definitions and the normal gameplay persistence records. Game saves continue to work and may keep gameplay state affected by live edits; this mode protects project source data, not save slots.

Stopping, natural exit or a launch failure restores the project map view and the map selected before Play, and discards the temporary snapshots. The game in an **Individual Window** keeps running while the editor has focus.

## Reload Lua while running

Save the changed Lua source files in your external editor, enter `$r` in the Console, then press `Enter` or **Send**. This updates existing functions while preserving the scene, objects and runtime state. The game must be launched from the editor and use loose Lua sources.

The Console reports the result. Changes to data or module structure may require a restart; see [Lua hot reload](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md#lua-hot-reload>) for the supported changes and the failure handling.

## Packaging

Choose **File → Pack Project**, select the target and follow the packaging log. The project must have a valid entry script and a compatible template. Define exactly one top-level `local APP_NAME` in `Scripts/Entry.lua` as a non-empty static string literal unique to the game, without control characters or later reassignment. Packaging rejects the sample value `LudorkSample`, a missing definition and expressions that require executing Lua to determine the name.

If packaging reports that access to an output path was denied, close any running copy of the packaged game and File Explorer windows on the output folder, then retry. Language servers and antivirus software can also hold generated files open.

The editor requires absolute signing-material paths without NUL, carriage returns or line feeds. Signing dialogs check that the files are readable before accepting them. Loading or saving a credential also validates its keystore or certificate path. Signing aliases and passwords must contain no NUL or line breaks.

Mobile and macOS application display names use the raw `title.value` text from `Data/Configs/System.json`. The title must be non-empty and contain no control characters; packaging does not resolve localisation keys. `APP_NAME` supplies the stable application and bundle identifiers and the sanitised `<game-name>` filename component. Changing the title or version does not change the installed application's identity; changing `APP_NAME` can require new signing or provisioning setup.

Each editor Pack performs one complete Export, including Export hooks and UI generation, before continuing with before-Pack hooks and packaging. Official Locale Tools uses its before-Pack hook only to exclude `Data/Locale/Locale.xlsx`. Direct command-line run and pack consume files exported beforehand; they keep their validation but do not perform complete Export or implicit UI generation.

**Encrypt game data** controls script compilation and shader, JSON and save encryption, and a partial selection shows its indeterminate state. **Encrypt save contents** sets the C++ Source runtime default. Standalone projects configure it through `SAVE_AS_LDC` in `Scripts/Entry.lua`. See [Saves](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/Runtime Data Configuration and Saves.md#saves>) for the timing and format rules. The `.ldpak` option is independent of encryption. Data encryption converts staged JSON values to compressed, obfuscated binary `.ldc`; source JSON stays editable. Rebuild packages containing the old compressed-JSON LDC format.

Packaging requires a valid project preview registry. See [Project preview artefacts](<../Native C++ Development/Native UI Adapters.md#project-preview-artefacts>) for preparing the preview runtime.

Packaging works on a staging copy and leaves project sources unchanged. It removes development files, preview-only binaries, project-root `EditorCache`/`Cache` and UI `editor` design data. UI asset keys remain extensionless and Controller references keep their logical Lua module paths, whether Data is stored as JSON, encrypted `.ldc` or in an archive. Directories named `EditorCache` or `Cache` inside `Assets`, `Data` or `Scripts` remain ordinary project content.

### Release version and internal packages

Set **Release version** in Pack Options. C++ Source projects also show **Internal test package (dev)**. The window reads `Main.proj` fields `packaging.version` and, for C++ Source projects, `packaging.dev`, defaulting to `"1.0.0"` and `false`. Confirming valid options saves the version and the applicable dev setting; cancelling writes nothing. Standalone projects always save `packaging.dev=false`, including when an older project has `true`. The version is three non-negative decimal components, such as `1.0.0` or `0.1.0`, up to 127 bytes, with no `v` prefix, leading zeroes, date suffix or prerelease suffix. Version metadata is not defined in Entry.

All game packaging commands accept `--version 1.0.0` and `--release`. C++ Source projects also accept `--dev`; either channel option overrides `packaging.dev` for that invocation only. Standalone projects always package as releases, ignore an older `packaging.dev=true` value and reject an explicit `--dev`. Command-line options do not write back to the project.

The packer captures one UTC+8 build time at the start and reuses it through every stage. Formal packages use the base version as their full release identifier. A dev package appends `YYYYMMDDHH` to it: at `2026-01-01T07:00:00+08:00`, version `1.0.0` becomes `1.0.0.2026010107`, using the build time captured at packaging start. dev does not change Release optimisation, signing, encryption or installation identity.

| Platform field | Value in both modes | Example at the time above |
|---|---|---|
| Android/HarmonyOS `versionName`; Apple `CFBundleShortVersionString` | Base version | `1.0.0` |
| Android/HarmonyOS `versionCode` | `YYMMDDHH` integer | `26010107` |
| iOS/macOS `CFBundleVersion` | `YYMM.DD.HH` | `2601.1.7` |

Build dates are restricted to 2000–2099 and platform limits are validated before replacing an output. Rebuilding within the same hour uses the same build number; wait until the next hour when a new store build record is required. Package paths use `<game-name>-<full-version>` before the existing platform, architecture, variant and signing suffixes. Repacking the same identifier replaces that artefact; other versions and unrelated files remain.

The staging copy receives `Data/BuildInfo.json` containing `version`, `fullVersion`, `dev` and `builtAt` (an ISO 8601 timestamp with `+08:00`). Both dev and release **game packages** retain this file through the normal Data encryption and `.ldpak` flow; it is never written back into source Data. Application release versions are independent of the top-level [project compatibility version](<Project Settings and Asset Layout.md#mainproj>) and [save schema versions](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Default Gameplay/Runtime Data Configuration and Saves.md#saves>).

### Loose and packed output

Every platform keeps the runtime files, `Assets`, `Data` and the runtime `Scripts` as loose directories by default. The `.ldpak` option is clear by default. When it is selected, the complete contents of each directory become root `Assets.ldpak`, `Data.ldpak` and `Scripts.ldpak`. Archive entries retain paths relative to their original directory, so resource paths, Data paths and Lua module names stay unchanged. Encryption and Lua compilation run before archiving, and an archive does not encrypt its contents by itself. The option is independent of encryption. Mobile packages enforce the same loose-or-packed contract, and Android and HarmonyOS do not recompress `.ldpak`.

Resource packaging rejects symbolic links, case collisions, illegal paths and output conflicts. A package contains either all three loose directories (`Assets`, `Data`, `Scripts`) or all three root archives. Corrupt archives, missing roots, mixed layouts and old per-group archives are rejected.

Packaging removes the development-only `Scripts/stub` tree. Any other `.d.lua` file left under `Scripts` fails packaging.

### Windows and macOS

Windows output is `dist/<game-name>-<full-version>/Main.exe` with its runtime files alongside it. macOS output is `dist/<game-name>-<full-version>.app`, with its display name taken from the System title. A custom output directory replaces `dist` as the parent directory. The package directory and its ancestors must not be symbolic links or directory junctions.

Windows and macOS packages copy the runtime files, `Assets`, `Data` and the runtime `Scripts`. Standalone packages keep a root launcher and place the runtime binaries in the platform package directory (`Binaries` on Windows, `Contents/Frameworks` for a macOS app). FFmpeg notices and source-offer material are included where applicable; see [FFmpeg option](<../Getting Started/Project Templates.md#ffmpeg-option>) for the distribution requirements. Windows packages exclude PDB files; retain them with the corresponding build for debugging.

Selecting macOS shows **Sign Application**, which is clear by default. Leave it clear to sign with the identity configured in this machine's environment variables, such as `LUDORK_MACOS_SIGNING_IDENTITY`, `LUDORK_MACOS_SIGNING_CERTIFICATE` and the `LUDORK_MACOS_NOTARY_*` credentials; without them the app receives an ad-hoc signature. Select it to choose a `.p12` certificate with its password, an optional signing identity, and optional notarisation with either an Apple ID, its team ID and an app-specific password, or an App Store Connect key with its key ID and issuer ID. For that run, the dialog settings take precedence over environment variables. Notarisation signs with a real identity, submits the app to Apple, waits for the result and staples the ticket; it is rejected for an ad-hoc identity. Saved signing details are restored after selecting the same certificate. An ad-hoc signature provides neither distributor certificate signing nor notarisation.

### iOS

Selecting the iOS 16.3-or-newer target on macOS requires a C++ Source project, a full Xcode installation with the iPhoneOS SDK, and a completed first-launch Xcode setup. Selecting iOS shows **Sign Application**, which is clear by default. Leave it clear to use the signed-in Apple Development team, taken from `LUDORK_IOS_DEVELOPMENT_TEAM` when it is set, and let Xcode sign automatically. Select it to provide the team ID, a `.p12` certificate with its password and a `.mobileprovision` provisioning profile; the packer then signs manually with that identity and profile and rejects a profile whose team or application identifier does not match. For that run, the dialog settings take precedence over environment variables. The certificate and the profile are required together, and a saved record is restored after selecting the same certificate.

By default, iOS packaging only creates `dist/<game-name>-<full-version>.ipa`, and no iPhone needs to be connected. Select **Export to iPhone** to install and launch the app on the device as well. This mode requires exactly one physical device on the iPhoneOS platform, either an iPhone or an iPad, that `xcdevice` reports as available. Simulators do not qualify. Any unlock, trust or Developer Mode message comes from the device itself. After installation the device must also trust the developer profile, which currently surfaces as a signing error.

### HarmonyOS

HarmonyOS packaging requires a C++ Source project, Apple Silicon macOS and DevEco Studio with the OpenHarmony native SDK. Every HarmonyOS variant uses HarmonyOS 6.0.2 / API 22. Select **Mobile** for the OpenGL ES phone and tablet host, or **2in1** and then OpenGL (default) or OpenGL ES.

Selecting HarmonyOS shows **Sign HAP**, which is clear by default. Leave it clear to produce one arm64-v8a unsigned HAP in `dist`: `<game-name>-<full-version>-harmony-mobile-unsigned.hap`, `<game-name>-<full-version>-harmony-2in1-opengl-unsigned.hap` or `<game-name>-<full-version>-harmony-2in1-opengl-es-unsigned.hap`. Select it to choose a `.p12` keystore, `.cer` certificate and `.p7b` Profile, and enter the key alias and passwords. The key password defaults to the keystore password. A successful signed run publishes the corresponding `-signed.hap`; signing alone requires no connected device and does not install or launch the game.

Signing information can be saved on this machine and restored after selecting the same keystore. The editor saves the material paths and alias in `harmony-signing.json` beside `Ludork.ini`, under `~/Library/Application Support/Ludork` on macOS, and stores passwords in the system Keychain. Keep the signing materials outside the project and repository. Passwords and material details are redacted from packaging logs; no credentials or signing configuration are written to the generated HarmonyOS project.

Both Debug and Release Profiles are supported. The Profile must be valid, signed and match the project’s bundle name. If packaging or signing fails, the previous successful output is retained. Command-line options are documented in [tools/README.md](https://github.com/JasonLeon01/Ludork/blob/main/tools/README.md).

Select **Export to matching HarmonyOS device** to enable signing and additionally install and launch the signed HAP. Only device export invokes HDC and checks the target device's Profile authorisation. Mobile export accepts a connected device that reports `default`, `phone` or `tablet`, although the mobile HAP itself declares `deviceTypes: ["phone","tablet"]`. The 2in1 export accepts only `2in1`. Exactly one connected device must match the selected form, and devices of the other form may remain connected. A connected device whose type cannot be read aborts the export even when it is of the other form. The 2in1 OpenGL package requires `libGLv4.so` on the device. Some emulators omit it. The app reports the missing module and does not fall back to OpenGL ES, so use the OpenGL ES package on those images.

Retain the matching native build outputs for debugging; the packaged native libraries have their symbols stripped.

### Android

Android packaging is available to C++ Source projects on macOS with Android Studio installed in `/Applications` or the current user’s `Applications` directory. It requires SDK Platform 36, Build Tools 36.0.0, a complete stable NDK r27 or newer and host CMake 3.28 or newer. The highest qualifying NDK in the local SDK is selected. SDK and NDK tools must be installed separately. The APK targets API 36 and runs on Android 7.0 / API 24 or later in either landscape orientation. Packaging creates an APK without installing or launching it.

Selecting Android shows **Sign APK**, which is clear by default. Leave it clear to publish `dist/<game-name>-<full-version>-android-arm64-v8a-unsigned.apk`. Select it to choose a JKS or PKCS12 keystore, enter its alias and passwords, and optionally save the information on this device. The picker accepts `.keystore`, `.p12`, `.pfx` and `.pkcs12` files and detects the type automatically. The key password defaults to the keystore password, and a saved record restores the keystore path and alias automatically. Cancelling the dialog returns to Pack Options, and a successful signed run publishes only `dist/<game-name>-<full-version>-android-arm64-v8a-signed.apk`.

Saved records live in the editor's per-user settings directory, as `android-signing.json` beside `Ludork.ini`, and on macOS under `~/Library/Application Support/Ludork`. A record stores the keystore path and alias only, while passwords use the credential store of the operating system. Passwords are never written to the project, Gradle files or logs. Android itself requires an update to an installed application to carry the same signing certificate, so the device rejects an update signed with a different key.

Retain the matching native build outputs for debugging; the packaged native library has its symbols stripped.

## Related pages

- [Project Templates](<../Getting Started/Project Templates.md>)
- [Tilesets, Autotiles and Maps](<Tilesets Autotiles and Maps.md>)
- [Distribution](<../Plug-in Development and Installation/Distribution.md>)
- [Script Mixin Authoring Workflow](<../Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Script Mixins/Authoring Workflow.md>)

documents.title: Overview
documents.content:
# General Data Reference Overview

This group documents the General Data types that ship with the Game project. Every value in these tables is project data rather than an engine enumeration, so a project is free to redefine the same type. Each page is generated from the current schema in `Data/General`, states its source file, and lists that schema's fields, defaults and member events.

## Where the data lives

General Data is stored in the project's `Data/General` directory, one JSON file per type. The Game project contains exactly the seven files below.

| File | Page |
|---|---|
| `Data/General/Class.json` | [Class](<Class.md>) |
| `Data/General/Enemy.json` | [Enemy](<Enemy.md>) |
| `Data/General/Equip.json` | [Equip](<Equip.md>) |
| `Data/General/Item.json` | [Item](<Item.md>) |
| `Data/General/Player.json` | [Player](<Player.md>) |
| `Data/General/Special.json` | [Special](<Special.md>) |
| `Data/General/State.json` | [State](<State.md>) |

For the type structure and field options, see [General Data and Text Config](<../General Data and Text Config.md#type-structure>).

## What each page documents

| Page | Contents | Member events |
|---|---|---|
| [Class](<Class.md>) | The player class preset: display name and description, plus `slot` mapping equipment slot names to the equipment initially equipped in each slot. | — |
| [Enemy](<Enemy.md>) | Enemy statistics (`MAXHP`, `ATK`, `DEF`, `EXP`, `GOLD`), `drops` as Blueprint class paths with map-cell offsets, `special` parameters and the attack animation. | — |
| [Equip](<Equip.md>) | Equipment: icon, the `Class` slot key it occupies and `attrPlus` attribute modifiers applied while equipped. | `onEquip`, `onUnequip` |
| [Item](<Item.md>) | Inventory items: `usable`, shop `price` and the derived sell price, icon and `cost`. | `onDrop`, `onUse` |
| [Player](<Player.md>) | Player presets: the referenced `CLASS` member and the starting HP, attribute, experience, gold and level values. | — |
| [Special](<Special.md>) | Presentation-only records — name, description and icon — whose parameters remain in `Enemy.special`. | — |
| [State](<State.md>) | States, including whether `stackable` increases an existing state's stack count. | `onWalk`, `onHookTriggered` |

Project references are expressed directly in enum schemas: `Player.CLASS` uses `Enums.GeneralData.Class`, `Enemy.special` uses `Enums.GeneralData.Special` as its dictionary key, and attack animations use `Enums.Animation`. Their stored values remain strings.

## Brace-wrapped display strings

Display fields can contain locale keys such as `{WARRIOR}`. Resolve them when displaying text; see [Game Localisation Workflow](<../../Plug-in Development and Installation/Official Plug-ins/Game Localisation Workflow.md#runtime>) for formatting and language changes.

## Relation to the General Data editor

Edit schemas, members and ability graphs in **Database → General Data** (`F10`). See [General Data and Text Config](<../General Data and Text Config.md>) for the workflow and generated files.

## Related pages

- [General Data and Text Config](<../General Data and Text Config.md>) — the editor window, schema authoring and generated Lua
- [Game Localisation Workflow](<../../Plug-in Development and Installation/Official Plug-ins/Game Localisation Workflow.md>) — workbook, Export and runtime resolution of `{ID}` tokens
- [Blueprints, Common Functions and Actors](<../Blueprints Common Functions and Actors.md>) — Blueprint class paths referenced by these schemas

documents.content:
# Class

This reference is generated from the current Game project schema in `Data/General`. The values are project data, not an engine enumeration.

Brace-wrapped display strings are resolved as described in [Game Localisation Workflow](<../../Plug-in Development and Installation/Official Plug-ins/Game Localisation Workflow.md>).

Source: `Data/General/Class.json`

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Member events | — |

## Schema

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `string` | `""` | The display name of this class. |
| `desc` | `string` | `""` | The display description of this class. |
| `slot` | `Dict[string, string]` | `{}` | Equipment slot names mapped to the equipment initially equipped in that slot. An empty value leaves the slot unequipped. |

documents.content:
# Enemy

Source: `Data/General/Enemy.json`

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| Member events | — |

## Schema

| Field | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | `string` | `"NEW ENEMY"` | The display name of this enemy. |
| `desc` | `string` | `"NEW ENEMY DESC"` | The display description of this enemy. |
| `MAXHP` | `int` | `0` | The enemy's maximum HP. |
| `ATK` | `int` | `0` | The enemy's attack value. |
| `DEF` | `int` | `0` | The enemy's defence value. |
| `EXP` | `int` | `0` | The experience granted when the enemy is defeated. |
| `GOLD` | `int` | `0` | The gold granted when the enemy is defeated. |
| `drops` | `Dict[string, sf.Vector2i]` | `{}` | Item Blueprint class paths mapped to map-cell offsets from the defeated enemy. |
| `special` | `{ dict = "any", key = { enum = "Enums.GeneralData.Special", valueType = "string" } }` | `{}` | Special member IDs mapped to their typed parameters. |
| `ANIMATION_KEY` | `{ enum = "Enums.Animation", valueType = "string" }` | `""` | The animation played when the enemy attacks. |

## Editing notes

The Enemy schema declares no member events. Gameplay abilities handle defeat behaviour.

In `special`, the presence of the key alone enables `Compete`, `Hard`, `Magic`, `First`, `Flank` and `Blockade`, and each of them stores `""`. `Vampire` takes a finite non-negative number, and `Reborn` takes a non-empty Blueprint class path. `FixDmg` accepts either a finite non-negative number or a non-empty expression string. Only the string form substitutes the current player and enemy values into `{m<attribute>}` and `{e<attribute>}` before `Engine.Eval`. No other special value is evaluated.

Each `drops` key must be a Blueprint class path whose generated Actor derives from `Source.MapActors.Item`. The matching `sf.Vector2i` value is added to the defeated enemy's map position. The spawned Actor tag is derived from the Blueprint path and the absolute target coordinates. When an identical tag already exists, that drop is skipped and a warning is written instead of a suffixed duplicate.

documents.title: Lua Runtime and Modules
documents.path: docs/en_GB/Lua and Blueprint Scripting/Lua Runtime and Modules.md
documents.content:
# Lua Runtime and Modules

Ludork runs Lua 5.5 with Standard extensions, LuaSF and project-native modules.

Readers new to Lua can begin with [Lua Basics](<../Getting Started/Lua Basics.md>). Ludork-native language additions such as `class`, `bool`, `list`, `dict`, copying, filesystem helpers and `asyncio` are described in [Ludork Lua Advanced](<../Getting Started/Ludork Lua Advanced.md>). This section covers project scripting architecture rather than language syntax.

| Model | Best suited to | Primary source |
|---|---|---|
| Blueprint graph | Visual event and execution flow | `Data/Blueprints/*.json` |
| Lua class | Reusable systems and gameplay types | `Scripts/**/*.lua` |
| Script Mixin | Lua behaviour attached directly to a Blueprint class | `Scripts/Mixins/**/*.lua` plus same-name `_meta.lua` |
| Declarative UI | JSON assets and generated typed View trees | `Data/UI/Assets/**/*.json`, generated `Scripts/Internal/UI/**/*.lua` and matching stubs |
| UI behaviour | Handwritten foundations and business Controllers | `Scripts/Internal/UIBase`; private Controllers inside window modules; independent row and Scene `Controller.lua` modules |

A Blueprint inheritance chain uses either graph mode or Script Mixin mode. Do not switch modes within one chain.

## Entry and module order

`Main.ini` selects the entry script, normally `Scripts/Entry.lua`. Load the root native modules in the order shown below, finish the direct `require` calls, then declare aliases:

```lua
local Engine = require("Engine")
local GlobalCore = require("GlobalCore")
local GlobalFunctions = require("GlobalFunctions")
local Logging = require("Global.Utils.Logging")

local Input = Engine.Input
local System = GlobalCore.System
local ManagerFunctions = GlobalFunctions.Manager
```

The native `GlobalFunctions` module exposes `Components`, `UI`, `NodeGraph` and `Manager`. Lua Blueprint function libraries under `Scripts/GlobalFunctions` are separate modules, loaded with paths such as `require("GlobalFunctions.Math")`; they are not members of the native root table. Other modules use their full dotted path. Do not add directory-level `init.lua` aggregators. Outside Blueprint function libraries, delay a `require` to resolve a real dependency cycle, or at an explicit first-use boundary such as an optional window's factory. The owning scene or feature must define that lifecycle; ordinary dependencies remain direct imports.

Runtime modules under `Scripts/GlobalFunctions` do not call `require` at module scope, including for native modules. They resolve dependencies from functions on first use so Blueprint function libraries can load without cycles. Their Lua paths and exported names must not occupy the same `GlobalFunctions` paths as C++ bindings.

Static dependencies flow from the root native modules through `Scripts/Global` to `Scripts/Source`. Global modules must not require Source. `Scripts/Internal` and `Scripts/GlobalFunctions` can depend on project modules in `Source`. Generic infrastructure can resolve opaque module names supplied by data, but it must not hard-code a higher-layer business module.

Native resource suffixes are exposed through `Engine.ResourceFileConstants`; game map identities and Gameplay tags live in `Source.Configs.MapConstants` and `Source.Configs.GameplayConstants`. Public enums use the independent `Enums.*` modules described below.

At runtime, scripts use exactly one storage form: loose `Scripts` during development, or a root `Scripts.ldpak` in a packed release. Mixed, missing or invalid layouts fail during startup. Logical module and entry paths are identical in both forms.

Every Lua state exposes project modules through `package.preload` without replacing native modules. Script Mixins still load fresh on every execution. Standard filesystem APIs do not expose archive contents.

Packed Data remains available through the same logical `Data/...` paths. `Engine.loadData` and `Engine.dataExists` resolve missing `.json` paths to binary `.ldc` alternatives; JSON platform APIs use only the exact path. This is a read-only runtime boundary, not a general archive filesystem.

Each independently reusable class has its own module, and that module returns the class. A window module may contain its private Controller and export the UI through `Ui.DefineWindow`; see the [Declarative UI Authoring Workflow](<Declarative UI/Authoring Workflow.md>). Utility modules may group related helpers.

Access private members only through `self` or same-instance `super(..., self)` dispatch. For other objects, including chained and dynamic access, use public getters, commands or data.

## Enum modules

Each public enum has its own module beneath `Scripts/Enums`. Its constants, EmmyLua annotations and API documentation stay together in the source file, without a mirrored enum stub. A handwritten enum declares a local table of string keys and scalar literals, then returns that table. It has no dependencies, functions or class construction:

```lua
-- Scripts/Enums/StairDirection.lua
---@enum Enums.StairDirection
local StairDirection = {
    None = "None",
    Up = "Up",
    Down = "Down",
}

return StairDirection
```

Load an enum directly, for example `local StairDirection = require("Enums.StairDirection")`, then use `StairDirection.Up`. Blueprint metadata references it with `type = { enum = "Enums.StairDirection" }`; see [Metadata Schema and Decorators](<Blueprint Scripting/Metadata Schema and Decorators.md>) for the full rules.

| Game enum module | Values or purpose |
|---|---|
| `Enums.StairDirection` | `None`, `Up`, `Down`, stored as the same strings |
| `Enums.BattleResultCode` | `WIN = 1`, `CANNOT_DAMAGE = 2`, `LETHAL_COUNTER_DAMAGE = 3` |
| `Enums.CriticalResultCode` | `VALUE = 1`, `NOT_NEEDED = 2`, `UNKNOWN = 3` |
| `Enums.DamageHintLevel` | `NONE = 0`, `BATTLE = 1`, `MAP = 2` |
| `Enums.WindowTransitionProfile` | `DEFAULT = "Default"`, `MENU = "Menu"` |
| `Enums.ShopMode` | `BUY = "buy"`, `SELL = "sell"` |
| `Enums.EventKey` | `LocaleChanged`, `AbilitySystemChanged`, `PlayerChanged` event names |
| `Enums.AbilitySystemChangeKind` | `Attribute`, `State` payload kinds |
| `Enums.PlayerChangeKind` | `Inventory`, `Name`, `Map` payload kinds |
| `Enums.MovementLatentOutput` | `STARTED = 0`, `FINISHED = 1` execution output indices |

Native builds generate `Enums.Engine.*`, `Enums.GlobalCore.*`, `Enums.GlobalFunctions.*` and `Enums.sf.*`. Project data saves generate `Enums.GeneralDataKey`, one `Enums.GeneralData.<TypeName>` module per data type, `Enums.Animation` and `Enums.Particle`. The editor resolves these string enums from the current project catalogue before saving, including unsaved changes; runtime `require` reads the generated source modules. These generated modules retain their owning native declarations or database records as the source of truth; edit those sources and regenerate.

## Native modules and values

Standard globals such as `os.createDirectories`, `os.removeFile`, `zlib` and `base64` are host-installed and are not required. The host also installs the `SAVE_AS_LDC` default from `LUDORK_SAVE_AS_LDC`; project overrides are described in [Saves](<Default Gameplay/Runtime Data Configuration and Saves.md#saves>). `LudorkRuntime` is a native library, not a Lua module. Core bindings load only through `Engine`, `GlobalCore` and `GlobalFunctions`, and there is no `Runtime` or `CoreSystem` alias.

LuaSF registers the global `sf`. Use exact native values such as `sf.Vector2i.new(...)`, `sf.Vector2f.new(...)` and `sf.Color.new(...)` when an API declares those types. Native containers and ordinary tables are not implicit vector adapters.

## Asynchronous operation updates

The default `Scripts/Entry.lua` calls `GlobalFunctions.NodeGraph.initLatent()` to enable operation updates. Custom entry points must also call it, including for script-only gameplay. See [Lua waiting examples](<../Getting Started/Ludork Lua Advanced.md#cooperative-tasks-and-file-batches>) and [Blueprint execution](<Blueprint Scripting/Execution Flow Events and Variables.md>).

## Session lifetime

The main thread and coroutines in one Lua VM share a native session. Captured callbacks and opaque values survive yields but cannot cross VMs, and session shutdown invalidates them. Native host integration is covered in [Session and module lifetime](<../Native C++ Development/Build and Module Layout.md#session-and-module-lifetime>).

## Live Debug

Live Debug lets you change Actor state in an editor-launched game, including Actors created at runtime. Changes are not saved to project data or reapplied when instances are rebuilt. See [Live Debug](<../Editor User Guide/Run Debug and Package.md#live-debug>) for the controls.

## Lua hot reload

In an editor-launched game that uses loose Lua sources under `Scripts`, save the changes and enter `$r` in the Console. At the next Console update, between gameplay callbacks, the runtime updates loaded project modules and used Script Mixins while keeping the current scene, objects and Lua VM. Both Debug and Release builds support the command. Packed or compiled-only scripts do not.

Reload replaces existing named functions while preserving module and class identities, instance fields, module data, constants, defaults and captured non-function values. Changing a function body takes effect. Changing a class default requires a restart. Cached references to matched functions, including native callbacks, are redirected to new function objects. Existing anonymous callbacks and suspended coroutine frames keep their original bodies, although references to matched helpers are updated. Constructors and lifecycle callbacks do not run again.

Loaded modules and used Script Mixins must retain their export names, class bases, field and function kinds, native callback members and compatible captured state. Deleting one of these modules, or making an incompatible structural change, requires a restart. Adding or removing ordinary global accesses is supported. An unmatchable custom `_ENV` requires a restart.

The runtime compiles all Lua sources before it applies changes. Entry is checked but not rerun. New and unloaded modules remain available on demand through `require`. Metadata, declarations, JSON data, UI assets and native code are excluded. Existing [audio processors](<Default Gameplay/Resources Audio Video and Effects.md#audio>) keep their code until a new playback starts.

Syntax, compatibility or candidate-execution failures leave the existing definitions in place and report an error in the Console. External side effects from candidate execution cannot be rolled back, so restart after an error that may have changed native resources or shared objects. Keep module top levels to definitions and dependencies, and put resource creation and subscriptions in explicit startup or lifecycle functions. See the [Game entry sequence](<Default Gameplay/Default Template Overview.md#entry-and-modules>).

## Logging and errors

Runtime Lua logs through `Global.Utils.Logging`: `debug` for diagnostic detail, `info` for significant stages, `warning` for recoverable data problems and `error` for unrecoverable failures. Logging does not raise. Use `error` or `assert` when execution must stop.

Engine providers are installed explicitly during [startup](<Default Gameplay/Default Template Overview.md#entry-and-modules>), not by `require`. Missing or duplicate providers, stopped sessions and invalid return counts or types raise errors. Returning no values differs from returning one `nil`.

## Runtime, declarations and metadata

Lua files have separate owners:

- `.lua` files contain runtime behaviour and implementation-only annotations. Pure-data enum modules also carry their public type annotations and documentation.
- Mirrored `Scripts/stub/**/*.d.lua` files contain other public documentation and LuaLS declarations, with no runtime side effects or `require`. Native API enum types remain in their owning declarations, such as `Engine.d.lua` and `LuaSF.d.lua`.
- Same-name `_meta.lua` files contain pure editor metadata and never run as gameplay scripts.

A requireable declaration uses `---@meta` with its module path; for example, `Global/Pool.d.lua` declares `---@meta Global.Pool`. Global-only `Standard.d.lua`, `Class.d.lua` and `LuaSF.d.lua` use a bare `---@meta`.

The EmmyLua workspace keeps `Scripts/stub` as its module root and library. In `.emmyrc.json`, `workspace.moduleMap` maps `^Scripts[.]Enums[.](.*)$` to `Enums.$1`, allowing enum imports to resolve to their annotated sources while other public imports retain their stub declarations. Enum sources do not use `---@meta`.

See [Project Templates](<../Getting Started/Project Templates.md>) for which declarations templates and game packages include.

Standalone and C++ Source templates include a Windows VS Code configuration named `Ludork: EmmyLua Attach (Windows)` that attaches the `tangzx.emmylua` `emmylua_attach` debugger to a running `Main.exe`. C++ Source templates also keep the native `cppvsdbg` and `lldb` launch and attach configurations. The EmmyLua attach debugger supports Windows only.

## Related pages

- [Lua Basics](<../Getting Started/Lua Basics.md>)
- [Ludork Lua Advanced](<../Getting Started/Ludork Lua Advanced.md>)
- [Metadata Schema and Decorators](<Blueprint Scripting/Metadata Schema and Decorators.md>)
- [Default Template Overview](<Default Gameplay/Default Template Overview.md>)
